article_title: Integrating Mathematical Thinking Into Family Engagement Programs
citation: Harris, B., Petersen, D., & Wulsin, C. S. (2017). Integrating Mathematical Thinking Into Family Engagement Programs. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/integrating-mathematical-thinking-into-family-engagement-programs
title: Tailor early math projects to a caregiver's language and culture
description: One of the seven tips gleaned from the grantees' experiences is to "tailor early math projects to a caregiver's language and culture." The principle holds that family engagement math activities work best when adapted to the language and cultural context of the caregivers who will use them with children, rather than delivered as generic materials.
requirements: Programs must know and attend to caregivers' language and cultural backgrounds when designing math activities.
constraints: This tip reflects grantee experience reported in the brief, not a tested comparison.
target_learners: Young children and their caregivers in family engagement programs
examples: The tip was gleaned from the experiences of the five Heising-Simons Foundation-funded family engagement programs described in the brief.
key_sources: Harris, B., Petersen, D., & Wulsin, C. S. (2017). Integrating Mathematical Thinking Into Family Engagement Programs. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/integrating-mathematical-thinking-into-family-engagement-programs

article_title: An Evaluation of the Teacher Advancement Program (TAP) in Chicago: Year One Impact Report
citation: Steven Glazerman, Allison McKie, Nancy Carey. (2009). An Evaluation of the Teacher Advancement Program (TAP) in Chicago: Year One Impact Report. Washington, DC: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: TAP's four-component whole-school design combining growth, leadership, feedback, and performance pay
description: TAP bundles four school-wide components: professional growth opportunities, promotion to school leadership roles without leaving the classroom, structured feedback, and performance-based compensation. The report describes it as "a whole-school intervention that aims to improve schools by raising teacher quality," evaluating whether these combined changes affect teachers and students.
requirements: Implementation across the whole school rather than for individual teachers only
constraints: First-year implementation in Chicago; effects on student outcomes may lag implementation
target_learning_goals: Improving teacher quality, support, and retention
examples: Chicago Public Schools implemented TAP beginning in 2007 in K-8 schools

article_title: Small class sizes for improving student achievement in primary and secondary schools: a systematic review
citation: Filges, T., Sonne‐Schmidt, C. S., Nielsen, B. C. V. (2018). Small class sizes for improving student achievement in primary and secondary schools: a systematic review. Campbell Systematic Reviews 2018:10. https://doi.org/10.4073/csr.2018.10
title: Target class size reductions at schools with high concentrations of socioeconomically disadvantaged students rather than implementing universal reduction
description: Because class size reduction is costly, the review's background argues it may be more economically efficient to concentrate reductions where benefits are largest. Evidence it cites indicates smaller class size is more beneficial for disadvantaged students, and STAR and SAGE evidence indicates minority, low-income, and educationally disadvantaged students benefited most. The review therefore suggests that "rather than implementing costly universal class size reduction policies, it may be more economically efficient to target schools with high concentrations of socioeconomic disadvantaged students for class size reductions."
requirements: Knowledge of which student groups benefit most from smaller classes, since the efficiency argument rests on differential benefit by socioeconomic background
constraints: The supporting evidence cited (STAR, SAGE) is described in the review's background rather than synthesised in this review's own meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in reading and mathematics
examples: The review cites the Tennessee STAR randomised controlled trial and Wisconsin's SAGE program as evidence that disadvantaged students benefited most from reduced class size
key_sources: Filges, T., Sonne‐Schmidt, C. S., Nielsen, B. C. V. (2018). Small class sizes for improving student achievement in primary and secondary schools: a systematic review. Campbell Systematic Reviews 2018:10. https://doi.org/10.4073/csr.2018.10

article_title: Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field
citation: Kara Conroy, Annalisa Mastri, James Wholley. (2021). Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Frame training and technical assistance as a partnership between provider and recipient, working with recipients to gather and incorporate their input
description: The brief recommends treating training and TA as "a partnership between the provider and recipient" rather than a one-way delivery. It emphasizes "how to work with recipients to gather and incorporate their input on the training and TA they will receive," so that TA is designed around recipient needs and developed using ongoing recipient input. This principle directs providers to build recipient voice into design, delivery, and iteration.
requirements: Ongoing mechanisms for gathering recipient input on the training and TA they will receive
target_learners: Training and technical assistance recipients in human services and employment programs
target_learning_goals: Recipient engagement with and ownership of training and technical assistance
examples: The brief presents strategies such as written TA requests, needs and assets assessments, and TA menus as ways providers work with recipients to gather and incorporate their input.
key_sources: Kara Conroy, Annalisa Mastri, James Wholley. (2021). Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/engaging-training-and-technical-assistance-recipients-lessons-from-the-field

article_title: Teacher Evaluation in Practice
citation: Sporte, S.E., & Jiang, J.Y. (2016). Teacher Evaluation in Practice: Year 3 Teacher and Administrator Perceptions of REACH. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. http://consortium.uchicago.edu/page/teacher-evaluation
title: Policymakers should take participant perceptions of an evaluation reform into account when building on strengths and correcting weaknesses
description: Because an educational reform's success "depends on how individuals involved in that effort interpret and act on that reform," the brief argues participant perceptions are key information about buy-in and implementation. Perceptions identify areas of strength and weakness from the experiences of those living with the system, so policymakers and practitioners should build on positive perceptions while addressing aspects participants see as needing improvement.
requirements: Systematic collection of teacher and administrator perceptions, such as annual surveys of those affected by the reform.
constraints: Survey responses are anonymous, so perceptions cannot be linked to individual evaluation ratings.
target_learners: Teachers and school administrators in districts implementing new evaluation systems
target_learning_goals: Successful implementation of teacher evaluation reform
examples: The UChicago Consortium surveyed all CPS teachers and principals annually across the first three years of REACH to track perceptions of fairness, usefulness, and burden.

article_title: Understanding the Experiences of LGBTQ High School Students in California by Race/Ethnicity
citation: Cerna, R., Stern, A., Austin, G., Betz, J., Zhang, G., & Hashmi, S. (2021). Understanding the experiences of LGBTQ high school students in California by race/ethnicity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/lgbtq-students-in-california/
title: Provide targeted social and emotional supports for LGBTQ students, using disaggregated data to mitigate disparities
description: The report argues that because adolescence is a critical developmental period, schools should use disaggregated well-being data to target supports for LGBTQ students. It states that "providing them with targeted social and emotional supports that foster positive development can be crucial" and that the data "contribute to understanding how the provision of key supports may help schools and communities mitigate disparities in student outcomes."
requirements: Schools and communities must have access to disaggregated data on student perceptions and experiences to identify where disparities lie
constraints: The report presents descriptive survey data; it does not test which specific supports produce which outcomes
target_learners: LGBTQ high school students, including transgender and sexual-minority students across race/ethnicity and Asian groups
target_learning_goals: Positive social-emotional development, school connectedness, safety, and academic outcomes
examples: The report identifies low parental-involvement promotion (no more than 35% among transgender students) and low school connectedness among American Indian/Alaska Native and Black transgender students (31%) as disparity points schools could address

article_title: Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department
citation: Jenna Howard Terrell, Sarah Barzee. (2023). Graduation Requirements and Measures: A Review of Performance Assessment Implementation in Select States for the New York State Education Department. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Table 1 summary of performance assessment implementation across Colorado, New Hampshire, Oregon, Rhode Island, Virginia, Massachusetts, and Vermont
description: Table 1 summarizes implementation across the seven case-study states on initiative, policy, rollout (voluntary or mandatory), purpose, subject and grade level, developer, common scoring rubric, and ongoing support. All seven states report assessments "Locally developed by educators." Rollout is mandatory in Oregon and Virginia and voluntary in Colorado, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, and Vermont; common scoring rubrics are reported as yes in Colorado, New Hampshire, Oregon, and Virginia, no in Rhode Island and Massachusetts, and in development in Vermont.
requirements: States differ in whether ongoing support exists: Colorado, New Hampshire, Virginia, and Massachusetts report ongoing support structures, while Oregon and Rhode Island report none.
constraints: Vermont's common scoring rubric and ongoing support are listed as in development phase.
target_learners: Students in grades 3 through high school across the seven case-study states
target_learning_goals: Demonstrating college and career readiness and content mastery through performance assessment
examples: Virginia's mandatory policy applies to grade 3 history and science, grade 5 writing, U.S. history to 1865, and U.S. history from 1865 to the present.

article_title: The Tapestry of American Public Education: How Can We Create a System of Schools Worth Choosing for All?
citation: Cookson, P. W., Jr., Darling-Hammond, L., Rothman, R., & Shields, P. M. (2018). The tapestry of American public education: How we can create a system of schools worth choosing for all? Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/tapestry-american-public-education
title: The tapestry framework: choice as a means to an end within a system of schools worth choosing
description: The report organizes American school choice as a 'rich tapestry' of four public option types—open enrollment (intradistrict and interdistrict), magnet schools, charter schools, and schools based on distinct educational models—each described with its history, scale, and evidence. Its central framing is that "School choice is a means to an end and not an end itself": outcomes depend on how options are designed and managed, not on the existence of choice. The framework reframes the policy question from choice versus no choice to what kind of choice, to what ends, with the goal that every child chooses, and is chosen by, a school worth choosing.
requirements: Systems of choice must attend to quality and access for neighborhood schools as well as novel options, since parents' preferred choice is the neighborhood public school
constraints: The analysis addresses United States public school choice policy as of 2018 and draws on two prior Learning Policy Institute documents
target_learners: All students in American public education systems
target_learning_goals: Universal access to high-quality, publicly accountable, equitably available schools
examples: The report's four lessons: make all schools worthy of being chosen, ensure access for all, promote diversity and inclusion, and leave no school behind
key_sources: Cookson, P. W., Jr., Darling-Hammond, L., Rothman, R., & Shields, P. M. (2018). The tapestry of American public education: How we can create a system of schools worth choosing for all? article_title: Building and Sustaining Talent: Creating Conditions in High-Poverty Schools That Support Effective Teaching and Learning
citation: Sarah Almy and Melissa Tooley. (2012). Building and Sustaining Talent: Creating Conditions in High-Poverty Schools That Support Effective Teaching and Learning. The Education Trust. https://edtrust.org/
title: TAP: The System for Teacher and Student Advancement
description: TAP is a whole-school reform model Ascension Parish implemented in two sanctioned high-poverty schools. “The TAP system focuses on four interrelated elements to improve teachers’ instruction”: ongoing applied professional learning, instructionally focused accountability, multiple career paths, and performance-based compensation. Evaluations inform professional development, advancement, and pay, and educators participate in regular collaboration and self-reflection within the school day.
requirements: Requires educators to participate in regular collaboration and self-reflection within the structure of the school day
Depends on rigorous performance evaluations perceived as tools to improve practice rather than punish
constraints: District officials report the four components were needed together; an associate principal said the school could not have improved “without all four components of TAP together.”
target_learning_goals: Improving instructional quality and student achievement in high-poverty schools
examples: Ascension’s Lowery Intermediate and Donaldsonville High left state improvement status, with Lowery earning a value-added score of 4, and the district expanded TAP to six additional schools.

article_title: Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future
citation: Charlotte Pierce. (2026). Strong Start, Strong Teachers: Supporting Teacher Preparation Programs for a Brighter Future. EdTrust-Midwest. https://midwest.edtrust.org
title: Talent Together registered teacher apprenticeship
description: Talent Together is a Michigan alternative certification program that "provides a free route to teacher certification and includes a registered apprenticeship to obtain paid work experience." It is a partnership between 56 intermediate school districts and 18 colleges and universities, prioritizes applications from uncertified current school employees in partner districts, and accepted 950 individuals in its first cohort while receiving 2,500 applications for 600 spots in its second cohort year. The report presents it as a promising path for growing and diversifying the teacher workforce.
requirements: Prioritizes applications from current school employees without teacher certifications who work in partner districts
target_learners: Current school employees without teacher certification in partner Michigan districts
target_learning_goals: Obtain teacher certification with paid work experience through a registered apprenticeship
examples: The first cohort was 24% people of color and the second cohort 41%, compared with 11.3% of Michigan teachers overall.

article_title: AI-Supported Lecturer Decision-Making in Higher Education: A Socio-Technical Perspective
citation: Köroğlu, M. N., Mayrhofer, J., Steinmaurer, A., Wintersberger, P., Dennerlein, S. M., & Weinhandl, R. (2026). AI-Supported lecturer decision-making in higher education: a socio-technical perspective. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00623-8
title: Taxonomy of AI-supported lecturer decision-making organized along four interrelated dimensions
description: The review develops an integrated taxonomy organizing AI-supported lecturer decision-making in higher education along four dimensions: lecturer decision types, AI system types, student data, and learning outcomes. As the article states, "the taxonomy organizes the field along four interrelated dimensions: lecturer decision types, AI system types, student data, and learning outcomes." It locates decision-making in the interaction among these dimensions rather than treating AI systems as isolated tools, and serves as a conceptual foundation for identifying dominant patterns and underrepresented areas across the reviewed studies.
requirements: Derived inductively via Mayring's qualitative content analysis from 27 empirical studies in higher education contexts
constraints: Categories were not mutually exclusive; a single study could be coded under multiple AI systems, decision types, data types, learning outcomes, methods, functions, and interfaces
target_learning_goals: Data-informed pedagogical decision-making supported by AI systems

article_title: Nursing Students' and Faculty Experiences with Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Qualitative Study Using the Technology Acceptance Model
citation: Arzu Akbaba, Afra Calik Kus. (2026). Nursing students’ and faculty experiences with artificial intelligence in education: a qualitative study using the technology acceptance model. BMC Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12912-026-04986-1
title: Technology Acceptance Model extended with affective and psychosocial dimensions for AI adoption in nursing education
description: The study uses the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a deductive framework with four constructs — perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, behavioural intention, and actual use — while remaining open to broader influences. Analysis found the four TAM constructs organised participants' experiences, but also surfaced "a dimension not anticipated within the original TAM framework": AI as emotional and psychosocial support. The authors argue this extends TAM's cognitive focus, aligning with calls for the model to better address emotional and social factors in emotionally challenging educational contexts.
requirements: Applied as a deductive coding framework with inductive subcategories allowed to emerge from interview data
constraints: The psychosocial dimension was a preliminary finding needing further empirical study, and was less evident among faculty members
target_learning_goals: AI adoption and integration in nursing education
examples: Four TAM-aligned categories (perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, behavioural intention to use, actual system use) structured the content analysis of 28 interviews

article_title: Unpacking the Heterogeneity of Pre-service Teachers' ChatGPT Acceptance: A Latent Profile Analysis Across STEM and Non-STEM Disciplines
citation: Pei-Hua Chen, Hsin-Yu Lee, Yueh-Min Huang and Ting-Ting Wu. (2026). Unpacking the heterogeneity of pre-service teachers' ChatGPT acceptance: a latent profile analysis across STEM and non-STEM disciplines. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00634-x
title: Integrated TAM–UTAUT2 five-construct framework for person-centered analysis of generative AI acceptance
description: The study integrates the Technology Acceptance Model with UTAUT2 to capture both individual cognition and context. As the article states, "The present study adopts three core TAM constructs (PU, PEOU, AT) and two contextual UTAUT2 constructs (SI, FC)". Performance and effort expectancy are measured with the established TAM scales to avoid redundancy, and consumer-oriented UTAUT2 components are dropped as less relevant to teachers' professional settings. The five constructs serve as LPA indicators, with behavioral intention as a distal outcome.
requirements: Measured via a contextualized questionnaire referencing ChatGPT and teaching-related tasks, validated by expert content review
constraints: The article notes CFA was not conducted, so factorial and discriminant validity evidence (AVE, composite reliability) is absent and future studies should incorporate CFA before LPA
target_learners: pre-service teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: understanding and differentiating pre-service teachers' acceptance of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT
examples: The framework structured the questionnaire (six constructs, five-point Likert items) and the LPA model in which disciplinary background was examined as a moderator of profile distribution

article_title: Evaluation of primary school teachers’ use and perceptions of artificial intelligence in primary school mathematics instruction: a mixed-methods study
citation: Ciğercci FM and Uygun N (2026). Evaluation of primary school teachers' use and perceptions of artificial intelligence in primary school mathematics instruction: a mixed-methods study. Front. Psychol. 17:1741116. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1741116
title: TAM and TPACK as complementary interpretive lenses for teachers' AI engagement and pedagogical integration
description: The study interprets teachers' AI perceptions through two frameworks used as interpretive lenses rather than statistically tested models. TAM holds that "users' beliefs about a technology—particularly its perceived usefulness and ease of use—shape attitudes and behavioral intentions related to adoption," explaining variation in willingness, attitudes, and engagement. TPACK and AI-related extensions interpret how teachers translate engagement into mathematics-specific practice, emphasizing that effective integration depends on the interaction of technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge.
requirements: Used to interpret, not to operationalize or statistically test, unmeasured constructs such as AI literacy or technological competence
constraints: The article states the frameworks are not used to infer unmeasured constructs; they provide a theoretically grounded vocabulary for interpreting documented relationships and accounts
target_learning_goals: Teachers' perceptions, reported uses, and pedagogical integration of AI in primary mathematics instruction
examples: The frameworks connect the quantitative examination of perceptions and background variables with the qualitative investigation of planning, implementation, assessment, feedback, and reported opportunities and constraints

article_title: To Tab or Not to Tab: Measuring Critical Engagement in AI Code Completion Tools Using Behavioral Signals and Attention Checks
citation: Jessica Hutchison, Ian Tyler Applebaum, Kenneth Angelikas, Kush Rakesh Patel, Phuoc Nguyen, Antonio Lazaro, Nicholas Rucinski, Rahad Arman Nabid, and Stephen MacNeil. (2026). To Tab or Not to Tab: Measuring Critical Engagement in AI Code Completion Tools Using Behavioral Signals and Attention Checks. Proceedings of the 31st ACM Conference on Innovation and Technology in Computer Science Education (ITiCSE 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3803400.3809394
title: Taxonomy of interaction behaviors with AI code suggestions
description: The article synthesizes fragmented prior characterizations of AI code completion interactions into a unified taxonomy of behavioral metrics. It organizes events into suggestion generation events (generate attention check, generate suggestion, suggestion shown), acceptance events (tab accept, slow accept), rejection and revision events (accept then modify, accept then delete, ignore), execution events (run code), and derived and aggregated session metrics such as acceptance rate, failed attention check rate, and average dwell time. The taxonomy operationalizes behaviors previously observed only qualitatively, such as slow accept, backtracking, and accept-and-adapt, so they can be captured quantitatively at scale.
requirements: Fine-grained event-level logging of suggestion generation, display, and user actions with timestamps
constraints: Developed and prototyped in a single CS1 course context with one problem type and one AI model; future work could more extensively interrogate sequential behaviors and interaction over time
target_learners: Novice programmers using AI code completion tools
target_learning_goals: Measuring and interpreting critical engagement with AI-generated code suggestions
examples: Applied to session-level Spearman correlation analysis of 55 students' interaction logs during the rainfall problem

citation: Dohn, N. B., Markauskaite, L., Huber, E., Wardak, D., Yang, H., Zeivots, S., Casey, A., van Diggele, C., Dohn, N. title: Classifications as boundary objects for cross-context coordination of GenAI practices
description: Drawing on Bowker and Star, the article frames classifications as boundary objects that are "customizable" and "ambiguous" yet have enough "common identities" to "both … travel across borders and maintain some kind of constant identity." The taxonomy provides a shared point of information and coordination from which educators and researchers with different expertise can take and impose meanings relevant to their own needs. It is intended for orientation and comparison rather than for creating specific learning designs.

Requires enough generality to allow comparison while retaining sufficient specificity to be useful
constraints: Not intended as an approach for presenting or creating specific designs for learning with GenAI
Classifications are suffused with ethical and political values; the proposal is only one possible way to look at the landscape
target_learning_goals: orienting search for good GenAI teaching practices
comparing GenAI learning activities across contexts
examples: Practitioners use the taxonomy to clarify what learning goals GenAI activities should support and what role GenAI should play

article_title: LecturaAgents: A Multi-Agent Framework for Adaptive Personalized AI-Assisted Learning and Embodied Teaching
citation: Jaward Sesay, Yue Yu, Siwei Dong, Börje F. Karlsson. (2026). Lect¯uraAgents: A Multi-Agent Framework for Adaptive Personalized AI-Assisted Learning and Embodied Teaching. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16428
title: Teaching Action-Speech Alignment (TASA) algorithm for generating coherent embodied teaching action sequences
description: TASA is the module that aligns embodied teaching actions with lecture speech. Per the article, "TASA uses a combination of LLM-based salience heuristics analysis and temporal semantic segmentation to help guide theTasaAgent with prospective relevant teaching action sequences." It segments slide contents and speech into labeled segments (Pedagogical, Personalized, Salient, Adaptive, Assessment), assigns each segment a Rough Notation or Handwriting action with a natural-language rationale, and outputs ordered action-speech sequences with word-level timestamps for the ProfessorAgent to execute during delivery.
requirements: Generated slides, scripts, and word-level speech timestamps (produced via Whisper ASR), plus a learner profile
constraints: The alignment module relies heavily on offline heuristics with a limited set of supported teaching actions, which may constrain richness of embodied instruction and robustness across diverse slide layouts
target_learners: high school, undergraduate, and graduate learners using the LecturaAgents delivery session
target_learning_goals: coherent, pedagogically informed embodied teaching actions synchronized with lecture speech
examples: The TasaAgent assigns segment labels such as Pedagogical, Personalized, Salient, Adaptive, and Assessment to slide regions and pairs each with an RN or HW action and rationale

article_title: Designing an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy: An Equitable and Transparent Learner-Centered Approach
citation: McCorkle, S. (2025). Designing an Aligned Generative AI Course Policy: An Equitable and Transparent Learner-Centered Approach. International Journal of Designs for Learning, 16(2), 96–110. https://doi.org/10.14434/ijdl.v16i2.41058
title: Task-inventory review pattern: inventory every step toward a finished product and ask what each task assesses
description: This pattern structures policy design around a complete inventory of student work. "The process begins with an analysis of student tasks by creating an inventory of each step a student would take that leads to a finished product of their learning." Each inventoried task is then reviewed by the instructor with the question "What, specifically, am I assessing?" Tasks that are not assessed but are simply a step towards a finished product are noted accordingly, which creates the basis for differentiated GenAI permissions across the course.
requirements: The instructor must create an inventory covering each step a student would take that leads to a finished product of their learning
constraints: Tasks that are not assessed, but are simply a step towards a finished product, must be noted accordingly for the pattern to distinguish assessable from intermediate work
target_learning_goals: alignment of course policy with what is actually assessed
examples: In the design case, the instructor reviewed each task in the inventory asking what, specifically, was being assessed, and noted unassessed stepping-stone tasks

article_title: Empowering teachers to use AI for differentiation: changes in teachers’ acceptance of AI-based technologies following participation in a short professional development training session
citation: Mesenhöller J and Böhme K (2026). Empowering teachers to use AI for differentiation: changes in teachers’ acceptance of AI-based technologies following participation in a short professional development training session. Front. Educ. 11:1875856. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1875856
title: Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as a framework for teachers’ social acceptance of AI-based technologies in schools
description: The article uses the Technology Acceptance Model, developed by Davis et al. (1989) and validated for teachers’ social acceptance of AI-based technologies in the school context by the authors’ prior work, as its organising framework. "The TAM posits that two main factors influence the acceptance of a specific technology: Perceived Usefulness (PU) and Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU)", which shape attitude, behavioural intention, and actual use. The SAELKIS questionnaire operationalises these constructs in three subscales (PU, PEOU, BI), and the study measures pre-post change on them.
requirements: Measured with a validated instrument (SAELKIS: PU 6 items α = .86, PEOU 3 items α = .90, BI 4 items α = .92)
constraints: Empirical studies in the school context suggest PU is particularly relevant for BI, whereas evidence for a direct association between PEOU and BI is less consistent

citation: Deliang Wang and Cunling Bian. (2026). Scaffolding Critical Engagement with GenAI: Transforming Ethnic Minority Preparatory Students’ Collaborative Discourse in Prompt Engineering Tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28630
title: For under-resourced learners, design targeted pedagogical interventions around human–AI collaboration rather than relying on technical training alone
description: The article argues that providing GenAI access and technical training is insufficient for ethnic minority and other under-resourced students, because without pedagogical guidance they may use GenAI as a shortcut that fosters cognitive complacency. The authors conclude that "technical training alone is insufficient; educators should design targeted pedagogical interventions around human–AI collaboration to avoid cognitive complacency and cultivate epistemic agency." The recommendation rests on the study's discourse, reflection, and self-efficacy findings showing scaffolding shifted students from passive consumption to critical co-creation.

citation: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842
title: Taklif.AI: an LLM-powered platform generating interest-based personalized college assignments
description: Taklif.AI is "a platform that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically generate personalized assignments tailored to individual student interests", distinguishing itself from platforms that personalize only on academic performance metrics by incorporating extracurricular interests and cultural context. It runs on a four-layer serverless AWS architecture (Next.js web layer, Lambda API layer, DynamoDB/S3 storage, and an AI layer using LangChain, LiteLLM and LangSmith) with Llama 3.3 70B as the primary model. The platform personalizes or simplifies assignments but does not evaluate submissions or alter core learning objectives.

constraints: The platform does not evaluate or assess student submissions, nor alter the fundamental structure or core learning objectives of assignments
Primarily tested on programming and mathematics assignments
Evaluation of actual learning outcomes is beyond the scope of the paper and planned as future work

article_title: TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring
citation: Dongjie Yang, Siyan Lin, Leixian Shen, Rui Sheng, Huamin Qu, and Zixin Chen. (2026). TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03952
title: TACT dual-taxonomy framework: a 13-strategy tutor-strategy taxonomy linked to a two-axis student-move taxonomy operationalizing conditional feedback decisions
description: TACT organizes ESL tutoring as a pedagogical decision space connecting learner-state annotation, tutor-strategy selection, and next-turn response generation. The student-move taxonomy records the learner's latest turn along two dimensions, move type and move status, where only Answer/Attempt moves can be Adequate or Problematic and other types are Non-evaluable. The tutor-strategy taxonomy "contains 13 strategies representing the intended pedagogical function of the next tutor turn", spanning prompting, backchanneling, affective feedback, verification, error flagging, hinting, guided revision, and direct correction. The mapping from student moves to strategies is conditional rather than deterministic, depending on proficiency, task difficulty, dialogue history, and prior support. Annotation reliability reached kappa of 0.708 for tutor strategy, 0.722 for move type, and 1.000 for move status.
requirements: Annotated authentic tutoring dialogue with codebooks and inter-annotator reliability checks to instantiate the two taxonomies
constraints: The article notes label abstraction is a limitation: real teachers blend instruction, affect, pacing, and rapport in ways a compact taxonomy does not always separate
target_learners: English-as-a-second-language learners across CEFR levels B1-C2
target_learning_goals: Conversational ESL proficiency through adaptive tutor feedback and scaffolding
examples: Expert annotators developed the coding scheme iteratively from 50 dialogue contexts, then independently double-coded 20 held-out contexts for inter-annotator reliability before corpus-scale annotation.

article_title: TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring
citation: Dongjie Yang, Siyan Lin, Leixian Shen, Rui Sheng, Huamin Qu, and Zixin Chen. (2026). TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03952
title: TACTCorpus and TACTBench: released annotated ESL tutoring corpus and strategy-balanced diagnostic benchmark
description: TACTCorpus is a model-assisted, human-audited resource derived from 260 authentic one-to-one English tutoring sessions from TSCC v2, containing 32,379 annotation records including tutor-strategy labels, student-move labels, and augmentation metadata, with a training split of 2,702 next-teacher-turn response-generation examples. TACTBench is a "strategy-balanced, optimization-aligned diagnostic benchmark" of 78 manually verified tutoring contexts scored on five rubric dimensions (Move, Agency, ESL, Tone, Conc.) plus accept, leak, and off-task judge flags. The article states it releases the data, benchmark, and model weights to support reproducible research.
requirements: Authentic anonymized tutoring dialogue as source data and quality-controlled annotation with codebook adjudication
constraints: TACTBench is designed around the specified TACT construct, so the article says improvements should be interpreted alongside disaggregated rubric dimensions, judge flags, and external transfer checks rather than as universal proof of better teaching

target_learning_goals: Pedagogically adaptive next-turn ESL tutor response generation

citation: Dongjie Yang, Siyan Lin, Leixian Shen, Rui Sheng, Huamin Qu, and Zixin Chen. (2026). TACT: Taxonomy-Aligned Post-Training for Pedagogically Adaptive English Tutoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03952
title: TACTutor: open 4B model post-trained with SFT and taxonomy-grounded GRPO for adaptive ESL tutoring
description: TACTutor is an open 4B model produced by post-training Qwen3.5-4B through parameter-efficient supervised fine-tuning with LoRA followed by taxonomy-grounded Group Relative Policy Optimization. The GRPO reward combines a mean normalized task score with grounding, format, and strategy terms plus judge-level penalties for unacceptability, answer leakage or over-helping, and off-task errors, with a KL constraint against the frozen SFT reference policy. The article says the reward is "transparent and auditable rather than an opaque optimization of a single benchmark score", and model weights are released.
requirements: A frozen pedagogical judge with hidden reference responses, gold taxonomy labels, and an evaluation rubric to produce reward scores and failure flags
constraints: The article states the main limitation is that next-turn response quality is not the same as long-term learning, since a locally well-scaffolded response's effect depends on learner motivation, prior knowledge, repeated interaction, and classroom context
target_learners: English-as-a-second-language learners, including local deployment on personal devices for privacy and latency
target_learning_goals: Learner-contingent pedagogical decision-making: selecting appropriate tutor strategies and levels of support in ESL dialogue
examples: Half of SFT instances include student-move hints in the system message while the rest preserve the dialogue-only setting; a best-of-n aligned SFT variant lets a pedagogical judge select high-quality candidate responses.

citation: Alex Liu, Min Sun, Lief Esbenshade, Victor Tian, Zachary Zhang, and Kevin He. (2026). Teacher-Authored Prompts for Configuring StudentAI Dialogue: K12 Classroom Implementation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16738
title: TASD: teacher-authored prompt layers as orchestration levers for configuring student-AI dialogue
description: TASD (Colleague AI Classroom Teaching Aide) frames student-AI interaction as a configurable classroom routine rather than an autonomous tutor. It uses a three-layer structure: a foundational LLM, a researcher-designed system-level prompt, and a top layer of teacher-authored prompts encoding local goals, plus a student-facing opening instruction. The article treats teacher prompts as "interaction design artifacts" that specify what students work on, how the AI structures participation, and what boundaries preserve responsible use, positioning teacher-authored prompt layers as levers translating pedagogical intent into structured dialogue.

constraints: The article notes the need for additional supports to reliably sustain higher-order reasoning during enactment, given the persistent DOK under-targeting gap

examples: In the Spring 2025 pilot, 16 teachers implemented 77 TASD activities generating 1,479 student-AI conversations with 878 unique students

article_title: AI-interaction literacy: reflections on how generative AI might be used to support self-regulated learning in higher education
citation: Linus Brunnström & Lisa Palmqvist. (2026). AI-interaction literacy: reflections on how generative AI might be used to support self-regulated learning in higher education. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602938.2026.2731261
title: Take-home assessments should emphasise evaluating knowledge at the qualitative phase of the SOLO taxonomy, with recall-based knowledge assessed in-class
description: Because GenAI is, in the authors' words, "a powerful tool for producing quantitative, factoid-type content", they propose that take-home assessments place strong emphasis on evaluating knowledge corresponding to the qualitative phase of the SOLO taxonomy. The rationale is assessment validity: a submitted artefact may no longer provide sufficient evidence of the student's own understanding when chatbots can produce plausible responses. Quantitative, recall-based knowledge is instead proposed for in-class formats where GenAI is not available as an aid.
requirements: Assessment formats such as take-home exams that explicitly promote critical thinking and independent problem-solving.
constraints: The proposal responds to the demonstrated risk that polished, multistructural AI output can be submitted as ready-to-submit text without indicating learning.

description: TAILS is a self-assessment questionnaire measuring language teachers' AI literacy across the six ED-AI dimensions. The initial version comprises 30 items (five per dimension) answered on a five-point Likert scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree, plus demographic items; the validated version is a refined 27-item scale. Example items include "I can collaborate with AI tools to design engaging lessons" and "I can decide when it is appropriate to use AI tools in my teaching and when not to." article_title: 'Problem-Based Learning and the Structural Conditions for Productive AI Integration'
citation: Michael Rowe. (2026). Problem-based learning and the structural conditions for productive AI integration. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/haet3_v1
title: Taste versus technique: judgement is the scarce capability when execution becomes cheap
description: Drawing on Rowe and Olivier (forthcoming), the essay distinguishes technique — the execution layer of knowledge work (searching, drafting, coding, formatting) that AI absorbs — from taste, the judgement layer: "the capacity to determine what is worth doing, to recognise quality, to distinguish the substantive from the merely competent." Taste cannot be offloaded because it requires contextual, values-laden, identity-informed reasoning. PBL is described as one of the few pedagogical structures that systematically requires taste.
requirements: Sustained engagement with consequential problems under conditions of genuine uncertainty, as well-designed PBL creates
constraints: What counts as relevant judgement is not culturally neutral; the framework names the layer of formation without settling what that formation should produce
target_learners: health professions students in higher education
target_learning_goals: professional judgement about what is worth doing
examples: Two nursing groups evaluating an AI-generated care coordination framework: the second group interrogates its assumptions about family availability and stakeholder perspectives, exercising taste

It states that "This further highlights the need for tailored scaffolds to guide students’ GenAI use styles and strategies", and that pre-service teachers may need support not only in how to operate GenAI but in clarifying why and when to use it during instructional design. article_title: Where Artificial Intelligence Enters Teacher Work
citation: Holster, J. (2026). Where Artificial Intelligence Enters Teacher Work. https://www.oecd.org/en/data/datasets/talis-2024-database.html
title: Design AI implementation and governance at the task level, attending to responsibility, data, oversight, and the checking work AI introduces
description: The article argues that because AI allocation differs sharply across professional tasks, adoption rates should not be treated as evidence that AI changes all parts of teacher work the same way. It recommends that "AI implementation and governance should be designed at the task level, with explicit attention to professional responsibility, student data, oversight, and the checking work introduced by AI use." It also warns against treating greater AI use as a normative endpoint for teacher development, since teachers retain responsibility for evaluating AI-supported work.

constraints: The large special-education association concerns reported use, not quality or benefit

verification and oversight of AI-supported tasks

article_title: Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2007). Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 509–539. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9054-3
title: Instruction should be tailored to the learner's level of prior knowledge or expertise
description: Because instructional effectiveness reverses with expertise, the review draws implications for "the design of learner-tailored instructional systems": instruction should be adapted to the learner's current knowledge level rather than fixed for all. The review presents this tailoring as the design consequence of the expertise reversal findings, with recent experimental attempts implementing the findings in adaptive environments. It applies wherever learner expertise varies within the target population.
requirements: Means of determining or tracking learners' current knowledge or expertise level so instruction can be matched to it
target_learners: Learners at differing levels of prior knowledge in a domain
target_learning_goals: Efficient acquisition of domain knowledge and skills
examples: The review discusses recent experimental attempts of implementing these findings into realistic adaptive learning environments.

article_title: The Expertise Reversal Effect
citation: Kalyuga, S., Ayres, P., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (2003). The Expertise Reversal Effect. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 23-31. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3801_4
title: Tailor instructional design, including gradually fading guidance, to the level of learner experience
description: The article's central instructional implication is that "instructional design should be tailored to the level of experience of intended learners"; otherwise, effectiveness "is likely to be random" and design recommendations "can be potentially quite counterproductive." As supporting practice, it reports that Renkl and colleagues consistently showed detailed worked examples suit novices but "should be gradually faded out with increased levels of learner knowledge and be replaced by problems," with fading superior to an abrupt switch.
requirements: Ongoing assessment of learner expertise in the specific domain so guidance can be matched or faded as knowledge grows.
constraints: Recommendations based on a particular design can reverse as expertise increases, so a fixed design recommendation is limited to its learner-expertise range.
target_learners: novice and more experienced learners in a domain
examples: Renkl, Atkinson, Maier, and Staley (2002) found that a fading-out procedure from worked examples to problems was superior to an abrupt switch.

citation: Doris B. Chin, Ilsa M. Dohmen, and Daniel L. Schwartz. (2013). Young Children Can Learn Scientific Reasoning with Teachable Agents. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2013.24

description: Taxonomy Betty is a variant of Betty's Brain in which students teach a computer agent by building concept maps with "type-of" and "has-property" links, then quiz the agent or enter it in the Triple-A-Challenge game. article_title: Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics
citation: Gregory K.W.K. Chung. (2015). Guidelines for the Design and Implementation of Game Telemetry for Serious Games Analytics. In C.S. Loh et al. (eds.), Serious Games Analytics. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4_3
title: Design game telemetry to target player behaviors that reflect the cognitive demands of interest
description: Because cognitive processes cannot be observed directly, inferences about their use rest on in-game behaviors and game states. The chapter states that "The game telemetry speciﬁcation should target player behaviors that reﬂect the cognitive demands of interest," where cognitive demands are the intellectual skills required to succeed in the game. A cognitive task analysis informs which mental operations to log, and game mechanics should be designed so that only players with knowledge of X can apply mechanic x, making mechanic x a potential measure of X.
requirements: A cognitive task analysis that provides insight about the mental operations players invoke during play
Precise definition of the behavior to observe and its connection to a theoretical framework
constraints: A specific behavioral act can manifest numerous underlying processes; judicious structuring of the interaction and capture of contextual information are needed to minimize ambiguity

target_learning_goals: measuring latent constructs such as adaptive problem-solving, decision-making, and content learning
examples: In a fractions game, the game should allow and log players' attempts to add fractions with unlike denominators rather than disallow the behavior, providing insight into misconceptions

citation: Gosse, C., & Van Reybroeck, M. (2020). Do children with dyslexia present a handwriting deficit? Impact of word orthographic and graphic complexity on handwriting and spelling performance. Research in Developmental Disabilities, 97(1), 14. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ridd.2019.103553
title: Tablet-based single-word dictation task of 40 words varying orthographic and graphic complexity
description: A digital-tablet single-word dictation task used to dissociate spelling from graphomotor performance. Children wrote 40 words whose "target words varied in orthographic complexity and in graphic complexity (simple vs. difficult)", and the task "was scored on spelling accuracy, handwriting quality and handwriting speed", allowing group comparisons across both complexity dimensions simultaneously.
requirements: Administered on a digital tablet so handwriting quality and speed can be scored
Word set must vary in both orthographic complexity and graphic complexity
target_learners: monolingual French-speaking children with and without dyslexia
target_learning_goals: assessing spelling accuracy, handwriting quality and handwriting speed
examples: Twenty-three children with dyslexia, 23 chronological-age matched and 23 spelling-age matched children completed the task

article_title: When do socioeconomic resources matter most in early childhood?
citation: Mollborn, S., Lawrence, E., James-Hawkins, L., & Fomby, P. (2014). When Do Socioeconomic Resources Matter Most in Early Childhood? Advances in Life Course Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.alcr.2014.03.001
title: Policymakers seeking to reduce inequality should increase attention on the early childhood years around age 4–4½, when socioeconomic resources matter most.
description: The authors' finding that SES–development relationships peak around age 4–4½ implies interventions targeting socioeconomic disadvantage should focus on this period. They write: "our results, which clearly point to a peak in the importance of resources around age 4 or 4½, suggest that policymakers interested in reducing inequality should increase attention on the early childhood years."
requirements: Programs must reach children before and during the prekindergarten year to coincide with the peak SES–development relationship.
constraints: The authors caution that more can be done beyond preschool: "new programs and research should also look beyond preschool for ways to reduce socioeconomic disparities."
target_learning_goals: Reducing socioeconomic disparities in cognitive and behavioral development
examples: The study found maternal education had the largest peak association (~0.4 SD) with cognitive scores, suggesting family resource interventions during this window may be especially consequential.

article_title: Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language
citation: Sung JE (2015) Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language. PLoS ONE 10(4): e0119424. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0119424
title: Task-demand manipulation framework for assessing sentence production: task type (memory demand) crossed with word-order canonicity (linguistic computational load)
description: The article proposes manipulating task demands along two axes to capture age-related change in sentence production: memory demands, via a memory-demanding syntactic-priming task versus a relatively memory-free sentence-completion task, and linguistic computational load, via canonical versus noncanonical word order in Korean. The tasks use "a very limited vocabulary used to construct a sentence" to minimize semantic-lexical top-down processing and isolate syntactic performance. The framework predicts that the condition combining the greatest demands best captures aging effects, which the regression results supported.
requirements: Speakers must successfully hold the prime sentence in memory until producing the target sentence for priming effects to occur
constraints: Developed and validated for Korean, a verb-final language with case markers and relatively free word order; canonicity effects may differ in languages with rigid word order
target_learners: elderly adults at risk for cognitive decline
target_learning_goals: detecting age-related decline in linguistic and cognitive capacity
examples: Examiners primed full passives such as "the Yellow is pushed by the Blue" and asked participants to describe a target picture using a passive with limited color vocabulary
key_sources: Sung JE (2015) Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language. PLoS ONE 10(4): e0119424. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0119424

article_title: Automaticity of word recognition is a unique predictor of reading fluency in middle-school students.
citation: Roembke Tanja C., Hazeltine Eliot, Reed Deborah K., McMurray Bob. (2019). Automaticity of Word Recognition is a Unique Predictor of Reading Fluency in Middle-School Students. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000279
title: Target automaticity in word recognition to improve fluency outcomes for struggling middle-school readers
description: The article argues that roughly half of struggling middle-school readers show word-level deficits despite adequate GPC knowledge, suggesting their difficulty lies in deploying knowledge automatically. It states that "an emphasis on automaticity may offer a useful target of intervention for those middle-school readers who still struggle with word-level skills." Because automaticity uniquely predicted fluency but not decoding or comprehension, intervention should focus on rapid, automatic activation of word meanings and phonology rather than additional decoding instruction.
requirements: Students must already have adequate knowledge of GPC regularities and sight words
Assessment must distinguish automaticity from knowledge, e.g., via masked vs. unmasked comparison
constraints: By middle-school, standards generally indicate no expectations for phonics or fluency instruction beyond Grade 5
The study is correlational; it does not test an intervention directly
target_learners: middle-school students below the 60th percentile in reading comprehension
examples: The study measured automaticity via backward masking in 56 middle-school students and found fluency-specific prediction

article_title: How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing
citation: Skagerlund K, Östergren R, Västfjäll D, Träff U (2019) How does mathematics anxiety impair mathematical abilities? Investigating the link between math anxiety, working memory, and number processing. PLoS ONE 14(1): e0211283. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0211283
title: Tailor math-anxiety interventions to the specific pathway being targeted (WM, number processing, or distal avoidance)
description: Because the study found MA operates through three distinct pathways — WM interference, degraded symbolic number processing, and a direct/distal effect — the authors recommend that interventions be matched to the pathway. They state one "possible way in which one might be able to leverage the current results would be to tailor interventions directed at each specific pathway", citing expressive writing for the WM route, exposure-based desensitization for the number-processing route, and early positive climate work for the distal route.
requirements: Assessment or theory identifying which pathway dominates for the learner and task type, since pathway strength varies with the kind of mathematical problem being solved
constraints: Recommendation is derived from a correlational SEM study of adults; the cited intervention studies (expressive writing, tutoring) are prior work, not tested in this study
target_learners: students in primary school (for early preventive intervention)
examples: The authors cite expressive writing before exams as lowering ruminating behavior and mitigating the WM drain, and intensive math tutoring as lowering amygdala activity in children with high MA

article_title: An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom
citation: Cuendet, S., Dehler Zufferey, J., Ortoleva, G., & Dillenbourg, P. (2015). An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10(2), 183–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9213-3
title: TapaCarp: a tangible user interface environment for training carpenter apprentices
description: TapaCarp is a CSCL environment based on a tangible user interface, designed from the start for classroom usage to help train carpenter apprentices. The article states the system "is based on a tangible user interface (TUI) and was designed to help train carpenter apprentices." It was deployed within a multi-step classroom activity in dual carpentry apprenticeships, where it was used only for a small part of the activity.
requirements: Designed for the constraints of the classroom environment from the start
Embedded in a broader classroom activity rather than used from beginning to end
constraints: A prior study found the tangible nature helped integrate it in the classroom but did not guarantee a meaningful learning activity
target_learners: carpenter apprentices in dual vocational apprenticeships
target_learning_goals: workplace-relevant carpentry knowledge and skills connected to apprenticeship practice
examples: Used in a classroom study with 3 classes of carpenter apprentices over two days for each class

article_title: Collaborating around the tabletop
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2011). Collaborating around the tabletop. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6:485–490. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9135-7
title: Tabletop environments as focal multimedia settings for small-group collaborative knowledge building
description: Stahl proposes tabletop educational environments as a hybrid of oral, literate, and digital interaction, analogizing them to conversation around a tribal fire. He writes that 'the tabletop can integrate physical and digital artifacts, spoken and written texts, and human and computational support to form a focal point, subject matter, and dynamic resource for collaborative knowledge building.' The framing positions tabletops as small-group rather than personal or whole-class media.
requirements: Apparent technological possibilities require considerable interface design, user evaluation, pedagogical structuring, and collaborative culture in order to achieve desirable educational results
target_learners: small groups of learners in classrooms, workplaces, or social gatherings
examples: The journal issue opens a flash theme of introductory papers on interactive tabletops in education

article_title: Collaborating around the tabletop
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2011). Collaborating around the tabletop. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6:485–490. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9135-7
title: Dillenbourg and Evans enumerate 33 research issues for tabletop computing clustered into four circles
description: The editorial reports that the overview paper by Pierre Dillenbourg and Michael Evans 'enumerates 33 such issues, clustered into the circles of: interaction with the individual student, support for small-group interaction, classroom orchestration, and institutional context.' The catalog highlights the complexity of tabletop interaction and counters the assumption that tabletops are simply more natural than laptops because of direct physical gestures.
requirements: The catalog is intended as a tentative set of central topics for analyzing tabletops in future articles of the flash theme
target_learners: students using tabletop interfaces in small groups
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning supported by tabletop computing
examples: The overview illustrates tabletop components with examples of diverse research prototypes

citation: Cress, U., Stahl, G., Ludvigsen, S., & Law, N. (2015). The core features of CSCL: Social situation, collaborative knowledge processes and their design. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 10, 109-116. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9214-2
title: TaraCarp tangible tabletop environment for carpenter vocational training
description: TaraCarp is a tangible user interface in the Cuendet, Dehler-Zufferey, Ortoleva and Dillenbourg study of classroom orchestration in vocational training for carpenters. "This top-down camera-projector tabletop system combines real and virtual artifacts." Apprentices cut a virtual object, print and improve plans, then pair up and cut real blocks according to each other's plans; the tabletops also serve as scripting and teacher orchestration tools.
requirements: Design based on detailed studies of how carpenters do their work, to minimize tacit-knowledge and school-to-work transfer problems
constraints: Further studies are needed to clarify how exactly students benefit from the collaboration
target_learning_goals: practical and tacit knowledge of carpentry plan marking and cutting
examples: Each student cuts an object virtually, prints the plan, exchanges plans with a partner, marks out a real block and cuts it according to the other learner's plan

citation: Mochizuki, T., Sasaki, H., Wakimoto, T., Kubota, Y., Eagan, B., Hirayama, R., Yamaguchi, Y., Yuki, N., Funaoi, H., Suzuki, H., & Kato, H. (2022). Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09382-w
title: Tangible puppetry tabletop role-play system with LED mood indicators and recorded bird's-eye animation
description: A tabletop simulation system in which a teacher puppet, student puppets, and props on transparent boxes with location indicators are used for microteaching role-play; a web camera and microphone under a semitransparent tabletop capture voices and puppet movements. Student puppets carry two-colored LEDs representing "distracted, focused, or normal" mental states, and the system "generates an animation based on the recorded locations, rotations, and conditions of each puppet" that is replayed for reflective discussion. In the study's triads, two student teachers played students with multiple puppets while one played teacher.
requirements: Requires the student-role participants to use their own school experiences to imagine a variety of students and improvise reactions without a script
constraints: The animation merely replayed the role-play and allowed reflection from multiple first-person viewpoints; it did not let learners simulate computational models of phenomena
examples: Triads of three student teachers performed 10-min role-plays with the puppets, then moved to a shared display to watch the recorded animation, sometimes stopping or jumping the video during reflection

article_title: How does collaborative task design shape collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation of learning? A study of secondary school students’ interactions in two varied tasks
citation: Zabolotna, K., Nøhr, L., Iwata, M., Spikol, D., Malmberg, J., & Järvenoja, H. (2025). How does collaborative task design shape collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation of learning? A study of secondary school students' interactions in two varied tasks. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09442-3
title: Design CSCL tasks deliberately, because task design—not technology alone—shapes collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation
description: The study argues that the nature of a collaborative task determines which collaborative processes students engage in: "the task design, not technology alone, significantly shapes students' learning interactions." Conceptually oriented tasks fostered prolonged cognitive engagement in building shared meaning, while hands-on tasks elicited frequent brief CKC episodes and more emotion–motivation regulation for sustaining positive collaboration. Designers should therefore anticipate the regulatory demands—cognitive or socioemotional—that a task's structure will create.
requirements: Explicit consideration of task structure, content difficulty, and technological setup when designing CSCL activities
constraints: Learners may radically reconfigure how a task is implemented, and actual implementation may differ from the teacher's original plan
target_learners: Secondary school students in technology-enhanced collaborative settings
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation of cognition and emotion–motivation
examples: The study compared a conceptual physics poster task on a shared interactive tabletop with a hands-on robot-hand building task and showed distinct CKC–regulation profiles for each

article_title: How a technology-augmented inquiry approach affects teacher practice and student learning in disadvantaged science classrooms
citation: Fan Chen, Gaowei Chen. (2026). How a technology-augmented inquiry approach affects teacher practice and student learning in disadvantaged science classrooms. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09788-1
title: Technology-augmented inquiry approach (TAIA): pedagogical visibility as a mechanism to scaffold student inquiry and reduce teacher orchestration load in disadvantaged classrooms
description: TAIA is the framing model of this study: a classroom orchestration system that integrates digital tools into the inquiry workflow so that "transient student thoughts into inspectable, actionable digital artifacts" give teachers pedagogical visibility. Its utility is described as twofold — scaffolding student cognition by decomposing complex tasks, and enhancing pedagogical orchestration by externalizing student thinking for the teacher. The article evaluates a context-adapted TAIA via the WeInquiry platform in two rural classrooms, arguing prior efficacy was established only in resource-rich settings.
requirements: Digital infrastructure sufficient for simultaneous classroom use (the school's network bandwidth supported a 40-minute trial) and student groups including at least one member with high ICT competency
constraints: Prior TAIA efficacy relied on assumptions of robust infrastructure, high student ICT competency, and strong prior inquiry experience, which rarely hold in disadvantaged settings
target_learners: eighth-grade students in low-infrastructure, high-need rural science classrooms
target_learning_goals: scientific literacy through inquiry-based learning: hypothesis formulation, controlled experimentation, and evidence-based argumentation
examples: In this study, EG groups each shared one tablet to access WeInquiry, submitting hypotheses, uploading multimedia experimental recordings, and completing CER-based arguments in a shared workspace while the teacher monitored progress in real time
key_sources: Fan Chen, Gaowei Chen. (2026). How a technology-augmented inquiry approach affects teacher practice and student learning in disadvantaged science classrooms. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09788-1

article_title: How design guides learning from matrix diagrams
citation: Jan van der Meij, Marije van Amelsvoort, Anjo Anjewierden. (2017). How design guides learning from matrix diagrams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9425-1
title: Tailor perceptual cues to the processing demands of the diagram rather than grafting them on arbitrarily
description: The article recommends that cues be matched to what the visualization actually needs: "Rather than arbitrarily grafting cues onto diagrams, the use of cues should be tailored to the speciﬁc processing demands the diagram poses". In matrix diagrams, arrows as organizational cues were overruled by the conventional format and content, so their use "should be considered with care". Designers should instead focus on learners' needs and the task, designing diagrams to facilitate effective encoding strategies.
requirements: Knowledge of the specific processing demands the diagram poses and of learners' needs and the task they are to perform
constraints: In matrix diagrams, arrows as organizational cues appear futile or even detrimental, since the matrix itself already organizes relations between two variables
target_learners: designers of learning materials with diagrams
examples: The experiment showed arrows did not guide initial reading behavior and had no effect on recall in four versions of a matrix diagram on personality disorders
key_sources: Jan van der Meij, Marije van Amelsvoort, Anjo Anjewierden. (2017). How design guides learning from matrix diagrams. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-017-9425-1

article_title: Investigating the role of an inquiry-based science lab on students’ scientific literacy
citation: Gülüzar Eymur · Pınar Seda Çetin (2024). Investigating the role of an inquiry-based science lab on students' scientific literacy. Instructional Science (2024) 52:743–760. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09672-w
title: Use speaking and writing as literacy tools within inquiry labs to support scientific literacy
description: The article argues that engaging students in meaningful scientific practices — argumentation sessions (speaking) and writing investigation reports (writing) — supports scientific literacy, because scientific literacy has both private and public views: understanding scientific knowledge individually and discussing and criticizing ideas with peers to reach consensus. The authors conclude that "scientific practices like ADI method should be used where students learn doing science rather than only conceptual understanding to develop students' scientific literacy."
requirements: Laboratory activities must include argumentation sessions, individually written investigation reports, and peer review so both speaking and writing function as literacy tools.
constraints: In the study the implementation time may not have been enough to provide important changes in scientific literacy of students.
examples: The experimental condition used five ADI laboratory investigations through 10 weeks, with argumentation sessions via a large whiteboard, individually written reports, blinded peer review, and report revision based on peer feedback.

article_title: How are Lao teachers’ goals for teaching associated with their instructional practices?
citation: Anongsack Mahavong, József Balázs Fejes. (2026). How are Lao teachers' goals for teaching associated with their instructional practices? Instructional Science, 54, 6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09756-1
title: TARGETS framework: Ames's TARGET dimensions extended with a social component
description: The TARGETS framework organizes instructional practices that shape students' perceptions of classroom goal structures into six TARGET dimensions — task, autonomy (authority), recognition, grouping, evaluation, and time — plus a proposed seventh social dimension. The article states that "a seventh dimension—the social component—has been proposed for inclusion in the TARGET framework, expanding the acronym to TARGETS." This study measured these practices with the Bardach et al. (2019) Goal structure questionnaire plus an adapted mutual respect scale, and modeled how teachers' relational and mastery goals relate to them.
requirements: Measured via teacher self-report instruments such as the Goal structure questionnaire (Bardach et al., 2019) and an adapted classroom mutual respect scale
constraints: In this study the time subscale was excluded and one item each removed from task, autonomy, and mastery-oriented instruction subscales for psychometric reasons; the authors note the framework's application to nuanced teacher practice may require refinement
target_learners: secondary school students in Lao PDR classrooms
target_learning_goals: shaping mastery-oriented classroom goal structures through teachers' instructional practices
examples: The study administered the Goal structure questionnaire (task, autonomy, recognition, grouping, evaluation, time items) plus an adapted mutual respect scale to 207 Lao secondary teachers.

article_title: Outspoken emotions – Emotion regulation during emotional challenges in collaborative learning
citation: Piia Näykki, Tiina Törmänen, Jaana Isohätälä, Hanna Järvenoja, Sanna Järvelä. (2026). Outspoken emotions – Emotion regulation during emotional challenges in collaborative learning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09815-1
title: Macro-script delivered on tablets prompting planning, monitoring and reflection phases of group work
description: The study used a macro-script as a discussion aid that made different parts of group work visible: the planning phase, the monitoring phase, and the reflection phase. Specific questions prompted discussion, such as "what kinds of feelings does the task evoke" in planning and "how has your work progressed" in monitoring. Questions were delivered via tablet computers, with the teacher announcing when groups could discuss them while groups decided the depth and length of discussion themselves.
requirements: Teacher instructions on tablet use at the start of each session and announcements of when to discuss script questions
constraints: The depth and length of the discussion was decided by the groups themselves
target_learners: first-year teacher education students in group work
target_learning_goals: structured collaborative discussion covering planning, monitoring and reflection
examples: In the case group's reflection phase, the script questions led members to describe obstacles related to group composition, timing and resources

article_title: Incorporating instructor presence in a multimedia language learning context
citation: Yu-Jr Lan, Emmanuel Manalo. (2026). Incorporating instructor presence in a multimedia language learning context. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09814-2
title: Before incorporating instructor presence into instructional videos, check whether the instructor's visible behaviors provide task-relevant information learners can directly use
description: The article recommends that instructional designers evaluate whether an on-screen instructor adds usable information rather than merely adding social presence. It concludes that "instructional designers should carefully consider whether the instructor's visual behaviors provide task-relevant information before incorporating instructor presence into instructional materials," because presence alone raised satisfaction and perceived learning but not performance. In this study the instructor's head gestures merely emphasized pitch diagrams already on screen, so the video was not a source of detailed articulatory guidance.
requirements: The instructor's visible behavior must convey information learners can directly use for the specific learning context and task demands
Learners may need appropriate strategies to effectively utilize the visual cues the instructor provides
constraints: In the study's tone-learning context, instructor modeling without additional cues to tone production did not improve measurable outcomes
Effectiveness may differ across domains and across content types within the same domain
target_learners: university students in online and distance education
target_learning_goals: second-language pronunciation and suprasegmental features such as lexical tones
multimedia learning outcomes in video-based instruction
examples: Fifty Japanese university students viewed lecture videos on the four Mandarin tones in which the only difference between versions was instructor presence, with head gestures that emphasized but did not duplicate on-screen pitch diagrams
