citation: Tessa Eysink, Sanne Dijkstra, Jan Kuper. (2002). The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016018210897
title: Tarski's World computer-based learning environment for teaching first-order logic
description: Tarski's World is a computer-based learning environment designed for teaching first-order logic (Barwise & Etchemendy, 1992), used in this study to teach the logical connective, conditional. In the experiment, instructions for 72 first- and second-year social science students were varied within it, including "a visual representation in which geometrical objects could be manipulated". It served as the delivery setting for the guidance and manipulation variables.
requirements: Learners work on problems about the conditional within a visual representation of geometrical objects that can be manipulated or imagined to manipulate
target_learners: first- and second-year social science students
examples: The study varied instructions for 72 students in Tarski's World across guidance and manipulation conditions

article_title: The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology
citation: Haataja, E., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., & Järvelä, S. (2021). The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 241–268. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09279-3
title: Tailorshop business simulation for collaborative complex problem solving
description: The Tailorshop is a computer-based business simulation in which "participants were required to run a shirt production company" by adjusting variables such as employee wages, storage costs, and shirt price to maximize company value. The article used its exploration phase, consisting of six simulated months, to elicit spontaneous monitoring interactions at month transitions, with each transition followed by a one-minute monitoring episode.
requirements: The task requires a desktop computer and is designed for small groups working face-to-face on complex system dynamics.
constraints: The study concentrated on the exploration phase only, not the performance phase of the simulation.
key_sources: Haataja, E., Malmberg, J., Dindar, M., & Järvelä, S. (2021). The pivotal role of monitoring for collaborative problem solving seen in interaction, performance, and interpersonal physiology. Metacognition and Learning, 17, 241–268. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09279-3

article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: Tailor self-report instruments to particular tasks or contexts, since broad-brush general measures strain validity
description: The article argues that most self-report questionnaires are very broad-brush measures that generalise across multiple times, situations and domains, and questions how fairly such instruments can capture the dynamic interplay characterising self-regulated learning. It recommends that instruments be tailored to particular tasks or contexts, and that the moment of self-report collection (straight after or even during task execution) be examined. Task-specific measuring connects to evidence that learning strategies differ by task type or subject.
requirements: Instruments aimed at a specific learning task that is representative of the tasks to be generalised
constraints: The distinction between task-specific and general measures relates only indirectly to the on-line versus off-line distinction
target_learners: learners studying expository or multiple texts in school and research settings
target_learning_goals: task-specific cognitive and metacognitive reading and study strategies
examples: All five special-issue instruments described are task-specific: a history-text studying questionnaire, a multiple-text reading inventory, an on-line sentence-by-sentence reading tool, a multiple-choice strategy measure, and calibration judgments tied to specific knowledge tests
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study
citation: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5
title: Task-generality account of metacognitive skills within self-regulated learning
description: The article organizes SRL components by task-specificity: cognitive strategies and motivation regulation strategies "are task-specific because they directly address particular kinds of information processing", whereas metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluating) are higher-order skills that regulate cognitive or motivational strategies within all kinds of learning tasks and are therefore task-general and transferable. This account motivates the hybrid-training approach, in which metacognitive skills are trained together with a task-specific cognitive strategy so they can later regulate new strategies in new tasks.
requirements: Metacognitive skills must be trained in combination with at least one specific cognitive strategy so learners can later recognize that the skills remain the same while strategies change across tasks.
constraints: The study's evidence covers fifth-graders trained with two cognitive strategies (conducting experiments, text highlighting) over one school year; the authors call for systematic variation of tasks and domains to prove transfer more broadly.
target_learning_goals: transfer of metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluating)
examples: The study trained metacognitive skills regulating either a control-of-variables experiment strategy (ME) or a three-step text-highlighting strategy (MT), then tested transfer to tasks requiring the other strategy.
key_sources: Schuster, C., Stebner, F., Leutner, D., & Wirth, J. (2020). Transfer of metacognitive skills in self-regulated learning: an experimental training study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09237-5

article_title: Metacognitive regulation contributes to digital text comprehension in E-learning
citation: Burin, Debora Ines; Gonzalez, Federico Martin; Barreyro, Juan Pablo; Injoque Ricle, Irene. (2020). Metacognitive regulation contributes to digital text comprehension in E-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09226-8
title: Task-referenced metacognitive regulation in e-learning reading: Global/Monitoring and Problem Solving as two regulatory dimensions
description: The article organizes self-reported metacognitive regulation of reading in digital e-learning comprehension around two dimensions identified by factor analysis. Global/Monitoring includes "having in mind the task purpose, re-reading and paying attention to important or difficult parts", while Problem Solving covers responses "in disorientation or lack of understanding, and the use of typography and navigation elements as comprehension aids". The framework is measured with a metacognitive inventory referred to the tasks just completed.
requirements: A metacognitive inventory referred to the comprehension tasks just completed, rather than a general dispositional questionnaire
constraints: Assessed with two low previous knowledge hypertexts completed at home in an e-learning environment rather than a class or lab
target_learners: College students reading expository digital texts in e-learning settings
target_learning_goals: Expository digital text comprehension in hypertext environments
examples: 219 college students reported metacognitive activities during comprehension tasks with a metacognitive inventory referred to the tasks just completed
key_sources: Burin, Debora Ines; Gonzalez, Federico Martin; Barreyro, Juan Pablo; Injoque Ricle, Irene. (2020). Metacognitive regulation contributes to digital text comprehension in E-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09226-8

article_title: Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities
citation: Gonny Schellings. (2011). Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities. Metacognition and Learning, 6, 91–109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9069-5
title: 58-item task-specific learning strategy questionnaire scored on a three-point frequency scale
description: A questionnaire constructed "straightforwardly on the basis of a taxonomy for coding think-aloud protocols", with all items referring to the specific history text read before completion and each of the taxonomy's categories tapped by one item. Items were scored on a three-point frequency scale ('almost never'=1, 'sometimes'=2, 'often'=3), a choice the article says may "reduce the variation in the choice of a reference point amongst students." The full instrument reached α=.87 (Study 1) and α=.79 (Study 2).
requirements: Items must explicitly refer to the specific learning task, and be formulated in vocabulary fitting the target students, using real protocol fragments
constraints: Subscale reliabilities were moderate to low in both administrations; the questionnaire is tied to one specific text-studying task
target_learning_goals: self-reported metacognitive and cognitive activities during text studying
examples: Example item: 'I tried to draw conclusions beyond the literal text', corresponding to the taxonomy category 'Inferring'
key_sources: Gonny Schellings. (2011). Applying learning strategy questionnaires: problems and possibilities. Metacognition and Learning, 6, 91–109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9069-5

article_title: Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts
citation: Ivar Bråten & Helge I. Strømsø. (2011). Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts. Metacognition Learning 6:111–130. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9075-7
title: Tailor strategy self-report inventories to a specific recently completed reading task
description: The article argues valid self-report measurement of strategies requires task-specific inventories rather than general ones, following four guidelines: administer a specific task the items refer to, give an instruction including reading purpose and a prompt to monitor strategies, administer the inventory immediately after task completion, and word items in the past tense without general stems. The authors note that general inventory scores "did not relate to comprehension performance, nor to the strategic processing reported on in a specific task context."
requirements: A specific task must be administered to which items refer; instruction must state purpose and direct monitoring; inventory administered immediately after task completion; items use past tense and omit general stems
constraints: Even task-specific self-reports focus on perceptions or memories of strategy use and may suffer from biased processing or reconstructive memory, with social desirability threatening validity
examples: The MTSI was administered immediately after the seven-text reading task, with items in past tense referring to that task
key_sources: Ivar Bråten & Helge I. Strømsø. (2011). Measuring strategic processing when students read multiple texts. Metacognition Learning 6:111–130. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9075-7

article_title: Effects of Family Literacy Programs on the Emergent Literacy Skills of Children From Low-SES Families: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Suzanne Fikrat-Wevers, Roel van Steensel, Lidia Arends. (2021). Effects of Family Literacy Programs on the Emergent Literacy Skills of Children From Low-SES Families: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654321998075
title: Design family literacy programs for low-SES children as targeted programs focused on a limited set of activities and skills, restricted to one (training) context
description: The meta-analysis concludes that low-SES children benefit most from family literacy programs that are targeted rather than comprehensive: "children benefit from targeted programs that focus on a limited set of activities and skills and that are restricted to one (training) context." The authors describe this as a "less is more" pattern emerging from several moderator effects. It applies to program developers designing interventions for families with low socioeconomic status.
requirements: Programs should focus on a limited set of activities and skills rather than a comprehensive mix.
constraints: Effects on follow-up measures were marginal (d = 0.16), so the principle rests mainly on immediate posttest results; the formal-activities and L2-training comparisons were based on only one study.
examples: The meta-analysis found shared-reading-only programs averaged d = 0.75 on comprehension-related skills, while programs combining all three activity types showed d = 0.13.
key_sources: Suzanne Fikrat-Wevers, Roel van Steensel, Lidia Arends. (2021). Effects of Family Literacy Programs on the Emergent Literacy Skills of Children From Low-SES Families: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654321998075

article_title: Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2
title: Taxonomy of linguistic and numerical task characteristics of mathematical word problems
description: The review organizes word problem task characteristics into two categories with named dimensions. Linguistic characteristics cover structure of the word problem (order-consistency, position of the unknown), schematic structure, semantic relationships, situational narrative familiarity, non-standard problems (unsolvable, multiple solutions, irrelevant linguistic information, realistic considerations), lexical consistency, code of numerical values, and length. Numerical characteristics cover number properties, required operation (additive vs. multiplicative, number of operations), solution strategy, relevance of information, and carrying. For schematic structure, "word problems fall into three additive (Total, Difference, Change) and five multiplicative categories (Equal groups, Comparison, Combination, Ratios and proportions, Product of measures)". Each dimension carries a presumable direction of association with performance.
requirements: Each dimension required at least five studies for robust variance estimation, since results "cannot be held reliable if there are under four degrees of freedom"
constraints: Multiplicative schematic structures could not be compared because too few independent studies investigated them; order-consistency, number properties, and other dimensions were dropped for the same reason
target_learners: Elementary school-aged children in Grades 1 to 6
key_sources: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2

article_title: Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2
title: Teacher as Social Context Questionnaire (TASC) and Situations in School Questionnaire (SIS) as measures of autonomy support and structure
description: The review identifies the two most frequently used measures of autonomy support and structure. The TASC (Belmont et al., 1988) comprises 41 items and three sub-scales (autonomy support 12 items, structure 15 items, involvement 14 items), usable as student or teacher report, with Cronbach's alpha 0.66–0.90 (student) and 0.73–0.90 (teacher). The SIS (Aelterman et al., 2019) is "a vignette-based questionnaire" with fifteen vignettes rated on a 7-point scale, with alpha 0.80–0.92 (student) and 0.73–0.85 (teacher). Both measure autonomy support and structure alongside their opposites, control and chaos.
requirements: Measures must include items operationalizing both autonomy support and structure for paired assessment
constraints: Studies in the sample varied widely in the number of items used, from 1 to 12 for autonomy support and 1 to 15 for structure
target_learning_goals: assessment of teacher autonomy support and provision of structure
examples: Student-report TASC sample items include 'My teacher listens to my ideas' (autonomy support) and 'My teacher makes sure I understand before they move on' (structure)
key_sources: Alexandra Patzak, Xiaorong Zhang. (2025). Blending Teacher Autonomy Support and Provision of Structure in the Classroom for Optimal Motivation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-09994-2

article_title: Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit
citation: Ann-Kathrin Krause, Jasmin Breitwieser, Garvin Brod. (2025). Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10087-3
title: Breaking entrenched strategy habits requires targeted disruption of cue-response links, not reflection or feedback alone
description: Contrasting habit theory with self-regulated learning models, the article argues that because habits are tightly bound to environmental cues, they are difficult to detect and disrupt. It states that "Reflection or feedback alone may be insufficient; targeted strategies are usually needed to weaken or replace entrenched cue-response links, a process that is both effortful and time-consuming." This supports interventions that restructure contexts rather than only informing students.
requirements: Sustained, deliberate effort over an extended time horizon to break cue-response links
constraints: The article notes this process is effortful and time-consuming, and that whether students' strategy reversion under stress is habitual or deliberate remains uncertain
target_learners: students whose ineffective strategy use is entrenched
target_learning_goals: replacing ineffective strategy habits with effective strategy routines
examples: The article cites qualitative reports from David et al. (2024) and Biwer et al. (2020) in which students found shifting toward more effective strategies difficult and fell back on entrenched habits, particularly under setbacks or time pressure
key_sources: Ann-Kathrin Krause, Jasmin Breitwieser, Garvin Brod. (2025). Understanding Learning Strategy Use Through the Lens of Habit. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10087-3

article_title: The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms
citation: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w
title: A two-axis classification of motivation interventions: targeted versus multifaceted focus, and add-on versus embedded implementation on a continuum
description: This paper proposes classifying motivation interventions along two independent axes: their focus (targeted, addressing one form of motivation or problem, versus multifaceted, addressing multiple forms) and their implementation mode — whether they are "embedded within the curriculum versus implemented as an "add-on" module or activity". The authors argue the add-on–embedded distinction operates on a continuum, from fully stand-alone lessons to in-depth reframing of curricula and instructional approach, and that the two axes are often but not always confounded. The classification is illustrated with examples in Fig. 1 and used to organize the paper's argument for multifaceted, embedded interventions.
requirements: The two axes must be treated as separable dimensions of an intervention rather than collapsed into one targeted-versus-multifaceted contrast
constraints: The authors present this as a conceptual proposal for thinking about interventions, not a tested taxonomy
examples: The paper locates targeted mindset and utility value interventions as typically add-on, and CORI and M-PLANS as multifaceted and embedded
key_sources: Linnenbrink-Garcia, L., Wigfield, A., Cabrera, L., Mouzaoir, S., McKinney, D., Liu, P. P., Marchand, G., Schmidt, J. A., Harris, C. J., & Guthrie, J. (2026). The Case for Multifaceted, Integrative Motivation Interventions Embedded in Classrooms. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10177-w

article_title: Measuring Children’s Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review
citation: Ritoša, A., Åström, F., Björck, E., Borglund, L., Karlsson, E., McHugh, E., & Nylander, E. (2023). Measuring Children's Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09815-4
title: Inventory of 77 established measures of young children's engagement in ECEC (Table 4)
description: The review compiles a categorized inventory of 77 unique established measures of child engagement in ECEC, grouped by measured concept (engagement, involvement, academic, social, task, joint, negative, reading, play, music, and computer engagement), with method (observation or survey), informant, and notes on subscales, dimensions, and school-age origin. It reports that "Of the identified engagement measurements, 202 relied on established measures of child engagement," and that five established tools were general observational protocols or software adapted to include child engagement. The inventory is presented in Table 4 with references in supplementary material.
requirements: Users should consult the supplementary reference list, as an existing citation indicated but did not guarantee that a measure was validated in earlier publications.
constraints: The review notes about one-third of established survey measures were primarily intended for school-aged children but were used in ECEC settings in the identified studies.
target_learners: young children attending ECEC, preschool, kindergarten, or pre-K settings
target_learning_goals: quantitative assessment of child engagement and involvement in ECEC
examples: Examples include the Leuven Involvement Scale for Young Children (LIS-YC, used in 15 studies) and the Individualized Classroom Assessment Scoring System (InCLASS, used in 22 studies).
key_sources: Ritoša, A., Åström, F., Björck, E., Borglund, L., Karlsson, E., McHugh, E., & Nylander, E. (2023). Measuring Children's Engagement in Early Childhood Education and Care Settings: A Scoping Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09815-4

article_title: Supporting Learners' Agentic Engagement With Feedback: A Systematic Review and a Taxonomy of Recipience Processes
citation: Winstone, N. E., Nash, R. A., Parker, M., & Rowntree, J. (2014). Supporting Learners' Agentic Engagement with Feedback: A Systematic Review and a Taxonomy of Recipience Processes. Educational Psychologist (in press). https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1359635
title: Design feedback interventions to target learners' recipience processes, not only feedback delivery
description: Because feedback benefits learners only when they actively receive, engage with, and implement it, educators should design interventions that build learners' recipience processes rather than treating learners as passive recipients. The review proposes the SAGE taxonomy (self-appraisal, assessment literacy, goal-setting and self-regulation, engagement and motivation) as "a theoretical basis for conceptualizing learners' responsibility within feedback dialogues, and for guiding the strategic design and evaluation of interventions." Intervention components such as peer-assessment, self-assessment, and engaging with grading criteria each map onto one or more of these processes.
requirements: Educators must diagnose which recipience process an intervention targets, since the four SAGE processes are empirically distinct and no two co-occurred systematically in researchers' rationales
constraints: Evidence on intervention effectiveness is largely descriptive and anecdotal; the review found no existing theoretical frameworks for categorizing recipience processes before SAGE
examples: The review catalogued 14 intervention component categories, including peer-assessment, self-assessment, and engaging with grading criteria, and mapped which SAGE processes each targets in Table 2
key_sources: Winstone, N. E., Nash, R. A., Parker, M., & Rowntree, J. (2014). Supporting Learners' Agentic Engagement with Feedback: A Systematic Review and a Taxonomy of Recipience Processes. Educational Psychologist (in press). https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2016.1207538

article_title: Teachers' Epistemic Cognition in Classroom Assessment
citation: Fives, Helenrose, Barnes, Nicole, Buehl, Michelle, Mascadri, Julia, & Ziegler, Nathan. (2017). Teachers’ epistemic cognition in classroom assessment. Educational Psychologist, 52(4), pp. 270-283. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2017.1323218
title: Table of Specifications (TOS) as a tool supporting epistemic cognition in test development
description: A Table of Specifications is presented as a reliable process teachers can use when constructing traditional summative tests. The article defines it: "A TOS is a conceptual and tangible table that helps teachers to align learning objectives with class time and expected cognitive levels of understanding." Teachers use it to determine the number and nature of test items so that multiple cognitive levels, low and high, are appropriately represented, thereby supporting alignment between objectives and the assessment event.
requirements: Learning objectives, ideally guided by a cognitive taxonomy, must exist for the TOS to align items against
target_learning_goals: developing summative tests that reflect multiple cognitive levels of understanding
examples: Dr. Jones could use a TOS when building a summative test for her learning theories unit

article_title: Mapping students' interest in a new domain: Connecting prior knowledge, interest, and self-efficacy with interesting tasks and a lasting desire to reengage
citation: Fryer, L. K., Shum, A., Lee, A., & Lau, P. (2021). Mapping students' interest in a new domain: Connecting prior knowledge, interest and self-efficacy with interesting tasks and a lasting desire to reengage. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101493
title: Task-Course-Domain refocusing of the Four Phase Model of interest development for university courses
description: The article refocuses the Four Phase Model of interest development (Hidi & Renninger) onto three measurable interest objects within a university course: Task interest (consistent with situational interest, with a specific task as its object), Course interest (a combination of interest in the learning environment and the content under study), and Domain interest (consistent with individual interest, not confined to a course). As the article states, "on the way to the development of an individual's Domain interest, for example, teaching, the student will encounter the specific localised levels of Task interest and the more general level of course interest within that broader domain." This structure makes it realistic to model interconnections between readiness, task experiences, and longer-term interest across a single course.
requirements: Readiness components (prior Domain interest, prior knowledge, self-efficacy) must be assessed to model forward connections to and through Task interest
constraints: Applied here to a mandatory introductory course for research postgraduate students new to the teaching domain
target_learners: research postgraduate students in an introductory university teaching course
target_learning_goals: development of Domain interest in teaching
examples: The study measured interest in seven strategically chosen tasks immediately after each task, Course interest in module seven, and Domain interest in the final module
key_sources: Fryer, L. K., Shum, A., Lee, A., & Lau, P. (2021). Mapping students' interest in a new domain: Connecting prior knowledge, interest and self-efficacy with interesting tasks and a lasting desire to reengage. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2021.101493

article_title: Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction
citation: Jelke van Der Pal, Tessa Eysink. (1999). Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction. Learning and Instruction, 9 (4), pp.327-341. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197363
title: Tarski's World: an instructional Interactive Graphical Representation System for formal logic
description: Tarski's World is described as "an instructional Interactive Graphical Representation System in formal logic". It exemplifies instruction that balances situativity and formality by relating a formal language to interactive graphics, thereby embodying the developmental situativity principle in which formal systems act as tools for situated, inductive learning. The system was empirically evaluated against only-situated and only-formal instruction for supporting conditional reasoning.
requirements: A formal language must be related to interactive graphics so the environment offers both situated activity and formal tools.
examples: Used in logic instruction as the combined situated-plus-formal condition against which only-situated and only-formal instruction were compared.
key_sources: Jelke van Der Pal, Tessa Eysink. (1999). Balancing situativity and formality: the importance of relating a formal language to interactive graphics in logic instruction. Learning and Instruction, 9 (4), pp.327-341. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197363

article_title: The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories
citation: Guo, J.; Bai, H.; Long, X.; Su, X.; Pang, W. (2025). The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories. Learning and Instruction, 99, article 102182. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102182
title: Task difficulty level as a mechanism bridging the Gestalt and perception-action theories of tool innovation
description: The article proposes that the Gestalt and perception-action theories differ in their assumptions about initial problem representations — a fixed, complete representation requiring sudden reconstruction versus a partial representation refined through exploratory interaction. The authors conjecture that "the Gestalt theory better explains the process of problems with lower task difficulty level" while "the perception-action theory better explains the process of problems with higher task difficulty level", because harder situations may overwhelm full representation. Task difficulty thus serves as the moderating mechanism reconciling the two accounts, tested via fixation and flexibility effects across tasks of varied difficulty.
requirements: Tasks spanning a range of difficulty levels relative to the sample, with difficulty indexed by success rate
Process measures coding fixation (repeating the same unsuccessful actions) and flexibility (shifting to novel actions)
constraints: Difficulty level is relative to the sample used; it was determined post-hoc rather than pre-determined
The flexibility-by-difficulty moderation held for ideal manipulation but not task success
examples: The study tested the conjecture by coding 139 children's exploration processes across nine tasks of varied difficulty and examining difficulty-moderated fixation and flexibility effects in multilevel logistic regressions.
key_sources: Guo, J.; Bai, H.; Long, X.; Su, X.; Pang, W. (2025). The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories. Learning and Instruction, 99, article 102182. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102182

article_title: COVID-19-related differences in students’ verbal achievements: Comparisons of different cohorts of students with SEN based on large-scale assessment data from Germany
citation: Rebecca Schneider, Sebastian Weirich, Poldi Kuhl, Stefan Schipolowski, Petra Stanat. (2025). COVID-19-related differences in students' verbal achievements: Comparisons of different cohorts of students with SEN based on large-scale assessment data from Germany. Learning and Instruction 100 (2025) 102228. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102228
title: Keep schools open as much as possible during disruptions and provide targeted support to students with SEN-L if school closures cannot be avoided
description: A forward-looking design recommendation drawn from the study's conclusion: schooling disruptions should be minimized for students with SEN-L, and where closures are unavoidable, targeted support should be provided. The article states, "it would be important to keep schools open as much as possible and to provide targeted support to students with SEN-L if school closures cannot be avoided." This follows from the finding that SEN-L students, who depend on additional support from teachers and personnel, showed steeper negative trends when such support was reduced during distance learning.
requirements: Targeted support mechanisms for students with SEN-L must be available when regular schooling is disrupted
constraints: The article notes many affected SEN-L students have already left the school system, limiting remediation
target_learners: Students with special educational needs in the domain of learning (SEN-L) in primary and secondary school
target_learning_goals: Verbal competencies in reading, listening, and orthography
examples: The study found fewer opportunities for targeted support for SEN-L students at regular schools during distance learning, which the authors link to steeper Grade 9 negative trends

article_title: An investigation on the value of drill work in the fundamental operations of arithmetic. Part II.
citation: Brown, J. C. (1915). An Investigation on the Value of Drill Work in the Fundamental Operations of Arithmetic. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/
title: Direct drill work toward the poorest pupils, where its effect is greatest and it reduces class variability
description: This principle holds that drill practice in arithmetic fundamentals yields its largest benefit for the lowest-performing pupils, and that drill decreases the variability of a class. The article reports that the effect of drill "seems to be greatest on the poorest portion of the class" and that drill classes improved from two to three times as much as non-drill classes. It supports using drill as a remedial and equalizing practice rather than only as extension for proficient pupils.
requirements: A drill period of repeated recitations on the fundamental operations (20 recitations in this study) with pre- and post-testing to identify the poorest pupils
constraints: The effect-size ordering is the author's hedged interpretation ("seems to be greatest"); the poorest drill pupils still averaged a negative gross gain of -3.1 points, so drill did not fully overcome their deficit
target_learners: elementary school pupils in arithmetic, especially the lowest-performing third of a class
target_learning_goals: accuracy and speed in the fundamental operations of arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division)
examples: The study compared the poorest 19 and best 19 pupils of drill and non-drill sections on first and second tests, finding poorest drill pupils moved from 50.7 percent below the drill-section average to 23.7 percent below it
key_sources: Brown, J. C. (1915). An Investigation on the Value of Drill Work in the Fundamental Operations of Arithmetic. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu/

article_title: Supplemental Material for Accomplishment in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) and Its Relation to STEM Educational Dose: A 25-Year Longitudinal Study
citation: Wai, J., Lubinski, D., Benbow, C. P., & Steiger, J. H. (2004). Accomplishment in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) and Its Relation to STEM Educational Dose: A 25-Year Longitudinal Study (Web Supplement). https://scholar.google.com
title: Table S1 taxonomy of 18 types of educational acceleration

article_title: Developmental change in the influence of domain-general abilities and domain-specific knowledge on mathematics achievement: An eight-year longitudinal study.
citation: Geary David C., Nicholas Alan, Li Yaoran, Sun Jianguo. (2017). Developmental Change in the Influence of Domain-General Abilities and Domain-Specific Knowledge on Mathematics Achievement: An Eight-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000159
title: Prioritize domain-specific mathematical skills, not domain-general abilities, as intervention targets for long-term mathematics gains
description: Because the importance of prior mathematical knowledge for further gains increases across grades while domain-general effects remain stable, the article recommends interventions focused on domain-specific skills. It states that "interventions focused on improving domain-specific skills, such as fractions knowledge, will likely yield longer-term gains in mathematics achievement than will interventions focused on domain-general abilities, such as working memory." Prerequisite skills identified include number knowledge and basic arithmetic in early grades and fractions knowledge in later grades.
requirements: Interventions must address the prerequisite domain-specific skills identified for the relevant grade band: number knowledge and basic arithmetic early, fractions knowledge later.
constraints: The data are correlational and do not support strong causal inferences; the article notes follow-up studies are needed to test whether improving domain-specific skills reduces individual differences in later achievement.
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement, number knowledge, arithmetic skills, fractions knowledge
examples: The longitudinal study indexed domain-specific knowledge with number sets, number line, addition retrieval, decomposition, and fractions comparison measures and showed their increasing importance across grades.

Developmental Change in the Influence of Domain-General Abilities and Domain-Specific Knowledge on Mathematics Achievement: An Eight-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000159

article_title: A meta-analysis showing improved cognitive performance in healthy young adults with transcranial alternating current stimulation
citation: Tae Lee Lee, Hanall Lee and Nyeonju Kang. (2023). A meta-analysis showing improved cognitive performance in healthy young adults with transcranial alternating current stimulation. npj Science of Learning 8:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00152-9
title: Neural synchronization and LTP-plasticity account for online and offline tACS cognitive benefits
description: The article proposes that tACS delivers "weak sinusoidal oscillating electrical currents" that temporarily synchronize neural firing timing with endogenous brain oscillations. Online-tACS is described as facilitating "higher entrainment between ongoing neural oscillation and external electrical oscillations," while offline-tACS "may cause longer lasting after-effects" related to LTP-type synaptic plasticity. This mechanism account explains why timing of stimulation matters and why performance (accuracy) rather than speed improves.
requirements: Stimulation frequency must be matched to the targeted endogenous oscillation frequency band
Weak-intensity sinusoidal current delivered via scalp electrodes
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation; the meta-analysis did not directly test entrainment or LTP mechanisms
Assumes the targeted brain regions host task-relevant oscillations
examples: In the meta-analysis, both online- and offline-tACS significantly improved cognitive performance, which the authors interpret as supporting the synchronization or LTP proposition
key_sources: Tae Lee Lee, Hanall Lee and Nyeonju Kang. (2023). A meta-analysis showing improved cognitive performance in healthy young adults with transcranial alternating current stimulation. npj Science of Learning 8:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00152-9

article_title: A meta-analysis showing improved cognitive performance in healthy young adults with transcranial alternating current stimulation
citation: Tae Lee Lee, Hanall Lee and Nyeonju Kang. (2023). A meta-analysis showing improved cognitive performance in healthy young adults with transcranial alternating current stimulation. npj Science of Learning 8:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00152-9
title: Meta-analytic evidence base of 56 tACS studies (93 performance and 32 reaction time comparisons)
description: The evidence base is a systematically assembled corpus: after searching PubMed, Web of Science, and other resources and removing duplicates and irrelevant articles, "the remaining 56 studies that examined potential effects of tACS on cognitive functions" qualified. These included 1797 healthy young adults (mean age range 18.0–33.0 years), 9 randomized controlled trials and 46 crossover designs, yielding 93 cognitive-performance and 32 reaction-time comparisons. Protocol parameters ranged from 0.7–3 mA intensity and 2 s–48 min session durations.
requirements: Studies must compare active tACS against sham control on cognitive performance or cognition-related reaction time
constraints: Cochrane risk-of-bias assessment flagged randomization, deviations from intended interventions, and outcome measurement; 41 of 56 studies did not mention blinding of experimenters or assessors
target_learning_goals: cognitive function measurement across executive, memory, perceptual-motor and language domains
examples: Frequency bands across the corpus: delta (4 studies), theta (30), alpha (19), beta (7), gamma (24), ripple (1)
key_sources: Tae Lee Lee, Hanall Lee and Nyeonju Kang. (2023). A meta-analysis showing improved cognitive performance in healthy young adults with transcranial alternating current stimulation. npj Science of Learning 8:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00152-9

article_title: Native learning ability and not age determines the effects of brain stimulation
citation: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y
title: Restorative-account and task-integration biomarker interpretation of the differential atDCS effect
description: The article proposes that atDCS acts restoratively rather than enhancively: performance change between the baseline block and the first training block "may indicate the ability of an individual to rapidly integrate task-relevant information", which "would be an indirect biomarker for the state of the neural components supporting the early stages of skill acquisition". Because the two blocks use different sequences, the integrated information is sequence-unspecific, such as number-to-finger mapping and interface properties. The authors link the effect to metaplastic properties of the motor network and to streamlined construction of inverse internal models.
requirements: Prior identification of parameters related to the mechanism to be treated for clinical use
Aggregated interaction between subthreshold atDCS and motor training-derived changes in synaptic efficiency to induce LTP
constraints: The estimation is indirect and limited to the finger-tapping task context
The mechanism through which the emergence of internal models could be streamlined is not clear
target_learning_goals: early-stage acquisition of sequential motor skills
examples: The authors note the detrimental effect in high-tier optimal learners resembles observations in highly trained individuals such as pianists
key_sources: Maceira-Elvira, P., Popa, T., Schmid, A.-C., Cadic-Melchior, A., Müller, H., & Schaer, R. (2024). Native learning ability and not age determines the effect of brain stimulation on motor skill acquisition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00278-y

article_title: Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep
citation: Whitmore, N. W., Bassard, A. M. & Paller, K. A. (2022). Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep. npj Science of Learning, 7:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00119-2
title: Targeted memory reactivation (TMR) with sleep-quality moderators (N3 duration and cue-evoked arousal)
description: TMR is a procedure in which "information that people learn is associated with a sound or smell during learning" and the same sensory cue is presented during sleep without waking the learner, after which "people remember information associated with the cue stimulus better than other information that was equally well-learned." The framework holds that cues reactivate specific recent memories during sleep and thereby strengthen them. This article extends the framework by showing TMR effectiveness for face-name learning depends on two sleep-quality factors: ample N3 (slow-wave) sleep duration and absence of cue-evoked arousal or sleep disruption.
requirements: Cues must be delivered during stage N3 sleep and at a volume not causing arousal
Learned material must be associated with a sensory cue (spoken names and background music in this study) during learning
constraints: The study could not determine whether benefits were due to the spoken names, the music, or both
Only one sleep session was recorded, so whether sleep-quality differences reflect stable individual differences is unclear
target_learners: adult learners (18–31 years old) in laboratory nap settings
examples: Participants studied 40 face-name pairs per class with distinctive background music, then during a nap half the spoken names from one class were presented at 10-s intervals with that class's music
key_sources: Whitmore, N. W., Bassard, A. M. & Paller, K. A. (2022). Targeted memory reactivation of face-name learning depends on ample and undisturbed slow-wave sleep. npj Science of Learning, 7:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00119-2

article_title: A brief tablet-based intervention benefits linguistic and communicative abilities in toddlers and preschoolers
citation: Peña, M., Vásquez-Venegas, C., Cortés, P., Pittaluga, E., Herrera, M., Pino, E. J., Escobar, R. G., Dehaene-Lambertz, G., & Guevara, P. (2024). A brief tablet-based intervention benefits linguistic and communicative abilities in toddlers and preschoolers. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00249-3
title: Ludic tablet-based fast-mapping game for word-object and letter-sound associations
description: A tablet game designed by a multidisciplinary team of early childhood educators, speech therapists, game designers, and cognitive neuroscience researchers, built on the fast-mapping paradigm. The main application taught 14 letter-sound associations and 59 infrequently used word-object associations across four to eight training sessions, each word-object association trained once to evaluate fast-mapping after a single exposure. Each trial comprised an encoding phase, a recognition phase, and, for preschoolers, a vocalization phase, with "contingent interaction, delivering immediate feedback to the children's responses". A tutor application allowed remote monitoring by a supervising educator.
requirements: A supervising early childhood educator to minimally oversee sessions and evaluate preschoolers' vocalizations
Tablets secured onto soft cushion-like supports, used individually in a quiet room setting
constraints: Training concentrated on uncommon word-object associations and letter-sound associations only, not all language features with semantic and grammatical contents
target_learners: Preschoolers (~42 months old) from low-income families
examples: In the study, children played four to eight sessions in nursery room environments, with the Control group playing only after the intervention finished

article_title: First-year students’ math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability
citation: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Sokolowski, H.M., Green, A.E., & Lyons, I.M. (2021). First-year students' math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability. npj Science of Learning 6:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00095-7
title: Interventions aiming to boost university STEM outcomes should target math anxiety specifically, not only math ability
description: Because first-semester math anxiety predicted both STEM participation and achievement over four years independently of math ability, and math anxiety accounted for roughly 40% of the math ability–STEM outcome associations, the authors argue that "future interventions developed with the aim of boosting STEM outcomes would do well to focus on math anxiety as a key leverage point". Focusing on math ability alone may fail to optimally boost STEM outcomes.
requirements: Interventions must be developed and tested empirically; the article provides impetus but does not itself test an anxiety intervention
constraints: The evidence is correlational/longitudinal, not an intervention trial; causal efficacy of anxiety-targeted interventions is not established in this article
examples: The study measured math anxiety at university entry and tracked four years of transcript data, showing unique predictive effects over and above math ability
key_sources: Daker, R.J., Gattas, S.U., Sokolowski, H.M., Green, A.E., & Lyons, I.M. (2021). First-year students' math anxiety predicts STEM avoidance and underperformance throughout university, independently of math ability. npj Science of Learning 6:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00095-7

article_title: A tailored small group instruction intervention in mathematics benefits low achievers
citation: Rosholm, M., Tonnesen, P. B., Rasmussen, K., Overgaard, S., Færch, J. V., Malm, S. G. & Harder, J. (2025). A tailored small group instruction intervention in mathematics benefits low achievers. npj Science of Learning 10, 18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00310-9
title: Tailored small-group mathematics intervention with screening, dialog-based teaching and an adaptive learning path
description: A 12-week small-group mathematics instruction intervention for the 20% lowest achievers, inspired by Math Recovery but with an adaptive learning path and assessment by the intervention teachers themselves. "Common to all of them was that they began with an investigative screening-test and -conversation, mapping pupils' understanding of mathematics, deficiencies (math holes) and their emotional perception of mathematics." Teaching was dialog-based, in 25–35 minute sessions four times per week, using specially developed materials, with teachers working to fill math holes and improve vocabulary, motivation and desire for learning.
requirements: Teachers participated in a four-day preparation course; coached arms added a three-day coaching course for the school mathematics coordinator
constraints: Only around 50% of the intended 48 sessions were actually held, particularly in grade 8 due to cancellations
target_learners: Low-achieving pupils in mathematics, the 20% lowest scorers in grades 2 and 8 in Danish public schools
target_learning_goals: Mathematics competencies across curriculum areas, including filling individual math holes, mathematical vocabulary, and motivation for learning
examples: Three variants were tested: 1-group (one teacher, 3–4 pupils), 1-group with coaching, and 1-1 with coaching; 1-1 without coaching had been tested in an unpublished 2014 intervention
key_sources: Rosholm, M., Tonnesen, P. B., Rasmussen, K., Overgaard, S., Færch, J. V., Malm, S. G. & Harder, J. (2025). A tailored small group instruction intervention in mathematics benefits low achievers. npj Science of Learning 10, 18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00310-9

article_title: Dynamic, continuous multitasking training leads to task-specific improvements but does not transfer across action selection tasks
citation: Angela D. Bender, Hannah L. Filmer, Claire K. Naughtin and Paul E. Dux. (2017). Dynamic, continuous multitasking training leads to task-speciﬁc improvements but does not transfer across action selection tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0015-4
title: Task-specific coordination account: dual-task gains arise from learning concrete stimulus-response associations for the practiced tasks
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that dual-task training benefits arise when the brain learns "how two speciﬁc tasks can be coordinated eﬃciently", via strengthened stimulus-response associations rather than generalized executive enhancement. The authors contrast this with the neuronal overlap theory, which predicts transfer when trained and transfer tasks share neural substrates; their null transfer results are described as inconsistent with the overlap account and in keeping with improved resource allocation in the practiced situation.
requirements: Exposure to the component tasks practiced in combination, so coordination of the two specific tasks can be learned
constraints: Gains do not generalize to action control tasks using new stimuli or different input modalities; the article notes its paradigm differs from video action games requiring intentional task-priority switching
target_learners: Healthy adults aged 18–40 in cognitive training studies
target_learning_goals: Multitasking and response selection under dual-task interference
examples: Participants trained on combined tracking plus discrimination for six sessions; gains stayed confined to the practiced dual-task condition

article_title: The gendered effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on adolescent literacy and schooling outcomes in India
citation: Nandi, A., Haberland, N., Kozak, M., & Ngô, T. D. (2023). The gendered effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on adolescent literacy and schooling outcomes in India. npj Science of Learning, 8, 42. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00193-8
title: Target remedial education programs toward poor and marginalized students to recover pandemic learning losses
description: This principle holds that after large-scale learning disruptions, remedial education programs should be directed especially toward poor and marginalized students, who bear the largest losses. The authors state that "Remedial education programs, especially for poor and marginalized students, are necessary for improving learning levels and reducing the longer-term risk of dropping out of school." The recommendation follows directly from their finding that literacy losses were concentrated among the poorest-quintile, rural, and disadvantaged-caste girls, and is reinforced by cited evidence that targeted after-school recovery programs in Tamil Nadu were highly cost-effective.
requirements: Governments must allocate more resources and improve the quality of education delivery to support learning recovery after school closures
constraints: The authors' own evidence is limited to 15–17-year-olds in India; unobserved differences between pre- and post-COVID groups may bias the estimates, and subgroup findings for boys may reflect inadequate statistical power
target_learners: Adolescents aged 15–17 in India, especially girls in poor, rural, and socioeconomically disadvantaged caste households
target_learning_goals: Foundational literacy (ability to read a complete sentence)
Schooling attainment and reduced dropout risk
examples: A Tamil Nadu state education recovery program of after-school learning sessions covering 3.3 million students recovered 28% of language and 21% of mathematics learning loss at a cost of US$7.6 per child per year
key_sources: Nandi, A., Haberland, N., Kozak, M., & Ngô, T. D. (2023). The gendered effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on adolescent literacy and schooling outcomes in India. npj Science of Learning, 8, 42. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00193-8

article_title: Stable, flexible, common, and distinct behaviors support rule-based and information-integration category learning
citation: Casey L. Roark and Bharath Chandrasekaran. (2023). Stable, flexible, common, and distinct behaviors support rule-based and information-integration category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00163-0
title: Taxonomy of category-learning behaviors: learning success, strategy, strategy consistency, learning speed, and learning stability
description: The article introduces a taxonomy of behaviors during category learning that decomposes individual differences into five measurable components: learning success (maximum cumulative accuracy), learning strategy (how a learner "uses underlying stimulus information to make decisions about category identity"), strategy consistency (the proportion of responses accounted for by the best-fitting strategy), learning speed (trials to reach a group-median performance benchmark), and learning stability (longest streak of correct responses normalized by total correct in a moving window of 50 trials). The taxonomy enables asking which behaviors are stable traits of an individual and which are flexibly modulated by the task, and which commonly or distinctly support success in RB versus II category learning.
requirements: Supervised category-learning tasks with feedback, so strategy models can be fit and cumulative accuracy, speed, and stability computed over trial windows
constraints: Consistency cannot be calculated for learners using random strategies; speed is undefined for learners who never reach the group median; stability is measured against modest overall accuracy in these tasks
examples: Experiment 1 illustrated the taxonomy with representative learners differing in maximum cumulative accuracy (92% vs 46%), consistency (92% vs 46%), speed (0 vs 282 trials), and stability (0.61 vs 0.32)
key_sources: Casey L. Roark and Bharath Chandrasekaran. (2023). Stable, flexible, common, and distinct behaviors support rule-based and information-integration category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00163-0

article_title: To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators
citation: René F. Kizilcec. (2023). To Advance AI Use in Education, Focus on Understanding Educators. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00351-4
title: Technology Acceptance Model: perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use as malleable determinants of technology acceptance
description: The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), introduced by Davis (1989), explains how an individual's perceptions of a technology influence attitudes and behavioral intentions, which in turn affect actual use. It treats "the perceived usefulness of a technology and its perceived ease of use" as fundamental determinants of acceptance, and holds that these perceptions are malleable through presentation, framing, design, and marketing. The article positions TAM as a foundation for a psychology of technology in education and calls for experimental tests of how framing, transparency, training, and context causally shape acceptance.
requirements: The model presupposes that user perceptions of usefulness and ease of use can be measured and influenced by how the technology is presented and framed.
constraints: The article states TAM does not account for the strong emotional responses that new technologies, especially AI-powered ones, can trigger among educators.
target_learning_goals: Understanding and shaping educator adoption of AI-powered education technology
examples: The article proposes using TAM to experimentally investigate causal effects of framing, presentation, transparency, training, and context on education technology acceptance, since prior education applications relied almost exclusively on structural equation modeling of survey data.

article_title: Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance
citation: Alvarez, N., Sanchez-Ruiz, A., Cavazza, M., Shigematsu, M., & Prendinger, H. (2014). Narrative Balance Management in an Intelligent Biosafety Training Application for Improving User Performance. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25, 35–59. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0022-z
title: Task Trees: hierarchical knowledge representation for task recognition and event selection
description: Task Trees are the knowledge structure used by both the Task Model Reasoner and the Narrative Manager in the Bio-safety Lab. A tree's root represents the whole task, intermediate nodes are subtasks, and leaves are Task-Level Events; sibling nodes relate through AND, OR and SEQ conditions, and leaf nodes marked as errors let the system recognize plausible but incorrect actions. The article states "A Task Tree is a hierarchical model which has a root node representing the whole task to perform on the top of the tree and child nodes being the subtasks in which it can be divided". Narrative Manager trees additionally mark system nodes with Balance, Impact and Closure parameters.
requirements: The spill-clearing task tree contains more than 250 nodes, so building one requires detailed protocol knowledge and expert annotation of error nodes
constraints: The article contrasts this with Death Kitchen's Danger Matrix, which allowed only one constraint (partial order) for event selection
target_learning_goals: Recognition and correction of user errors during protocol execution
Real-time monitoring of multi-step laboratory procedures
examples: The spill accident tree models bordering, covering, disinfecting, and waste disposal, with incorrect border-placement nodes that trigger warnings

article_title: A Recommender System of Postgraduate Courses Based on Soft Skills: A Psychometric-inspired Approach
citation: Luis Alberto Pinos Ullauri, Alexis Lebis, Abir Karami, Mathieu Vermeulen, Anthony Fleury, Wim Van den Noortgate. (2025). A Recommender System of Postgraduate Courses Based on Soft Skills: A Psychometric-inspired Approach. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00463-z
title: Targeted soft skill profile per specialisation represented as kiviat-style thresholds
description: A targeted soft skill profile is the ensemble of minimum expected proficiency targets for each soft skill, defined per program specialisation and represented as polygons of 10 sides (kiviat diagrams) showing the targeted threshold per skill. The article proposes it because demanded soft skills "may vary between degrees or specialisations", so different specialisations can carry distinct profiles. In the implementation, profiles were set to the students' average proficiency at stage 2 per specialisation.
requirements: Determination of the profile requires thorough debate with program stakeholders (teachers, labour market representatives, alumni, current students, the HEI)
constraints: The profiles used in the illustration were chosen for simplicity as students' average proficiency, and the article acknowledges profile determination is a study by itself
target_learners: students in specialisation years of an engineering program
target_learning_goals: meeting specialisation-specific minimum soft skill proficiency targets
examples: Example profiles: Specialisation 1 demands a balanced 2.5 out of 4 across all skills; Specialisation 4 has prominent peaks in soft skills 3 and 7

article_title: The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study
citation: Kogan, G., Chassidim, H., & Rabaev, I. (2024). The efficacy of animation and visualization in teaching data structures: a case study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10382-w
title: Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) applied to learning-tool adoption
description: The study applies the Technology Acceptance Model, which measures three key factors related to acceptance of a learning technology: perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEOU), and attitude toward usage (ATU). These factors are measured "to determine the level of acceptance and adoption of the AVDS tool and to provide insights into areas that need improvement." The model was tested via structural equation modeling with weight constraints across experimental conditions.
requirements: Multiple questionnaire items per construct with validity and reliability evaluation (Cronbach's alpha, AVE, composite reliability)
constraints: A minimum sample size of 200 to 300 observations is often recommended for SEM, but this study had 78 participants
target_learning_goals: understanding factors influencing adoption of learning technology
examples: TAM administered before and after the performance test to the experimental group and once to the control group

article_title: Improving K-12 Teachers’ Acceptance of Open Educational Resources by Open Educational Practices: A Mixed Methods Inquiry
citation: Hengtao Tang, Yu-Ju Lin, & Yingxiao Qian. (2021). Improving K-12 Teachers' Acceptance of Open Educational Resources by Open Educational Practices: A Mixed Methods Inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10046-z
title: Technology Acceptance Model (extended TAM 2/TAM 3) as a framework for K-12 teachers' OER acceptance
description: The article frames teachers' OER acceptance using the technology acceptance model, in which perceived ease (PE) and perceived usefulness (PU) determine intention (IN) with attitudes (AT) mediating. It extends this with TAM 2's social influence and cognitive instrumental processes — subjective norm (SN) and job-fit (JF) — and TAM 3's addition of self-efficacy (SE) as a determinant for PE. The article states PE "is also the most fundamental determinant of teachers' IN since it predicts PU and AT." The seven factors structured both the survey instrument and the deductive qualitative coding template.
requirements: The instrument adapted from Kim et al. (2015) measuring the seven factors on 5-point Likert scales
constraints: The article cautions teacher perception might be influenced by other factors, such as alignment with standards, grades, and subjects
target_learning_goals: Acceptance and integration of open educational resources in teaching
examples: The study measured PE, PU, AT, SE, SN, JF, and IN before and after a renewable-assignment intervention and used TAM theories as the a priori coding template for qualitative analysis
key_sources: Hengtao Tang, Yu-Ju Lin, & Yingxiao Qian. (2021). Improving K-12 Teachers' Acceptance of Open Educational Resources by Open Educational Practices: A Mixed Methods Inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10046-z

article_title: Factors contributing to teachers’ acceptance intention to gamified EFL tools: a scale development study
citation: Zhanni Luo. (2024). Factors contributing to teachers' acceptance intention to gamified EFL tools: a scale development study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10249-6
title: Six-factor framework of teachers' acceptance intention toward gamified learning tools
description: A conceptual framework synthesised from TAM, TAM2, TAM3, UTAUT and related models using grounded-theory grouping of TAM-expanding factors. As the article states, "attitude consists of four constructs: perceived enjoyment, perceived usefulness (PU), perceived ease of use (PEoU), and perceived risks", with PU containing four sub-constructs (relatedness, PU on engagement, PU on academic outcomes, social influence), PEoU containing four sub-constructs (accessibility, compatibility, complexity, user control), plus facilitating conditions and control variables. It served as the basis for item generation in the scale development.
requirements: Intended for measuring or studying teacher acceptance of gamified learning tools; the article notes it can be used or adapted for future studies in gamified learning
constraints: The EFA in this study retained only PU and PEoU, so the full six-construct structure was not statistically supported in this context

citation: Herodotou, C., Rienties, B., Boroowa, A., Zdrahal, Z., & Hlosta, M. (2019). A large-scale implementation of predictive learning analytics in higher education: the teachers' role and perspective. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 1273–1306. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09685-0
title: Technology Acceptance Model and Academic Resistance Model as combined lenses on teachers' PLA adoption
description: The article uses the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Academic Resistance Model (ARM) together to explain why some teachers engage with predictive learning analytics. TAM explains usage via "perceived usefulness" and "perceived ease of use"; ARM explains resistance through three attitude dimensions: cognitive (beliefs about PLA accuracy), emotional (feelings about being monitored or replaced), and intentional (plans to use or resist the technology). The authors argue the models complement each other, with perceived usefulness overlapping cognitive attitudes and anxiety about complexity spanning both models.

examples: Interview questions were organised around TAM pillars (impact on teaching, ease of use) and ARM pillars (concerns and feelings, future intentions)

title: Computerized tablet-administered dynamic series completion test with graduated prompts
description: A newly developed computerized visual-spatial series completion test for 6–8-year-olds, administered on an Acer Aspire Switch 10 tablet and programmed in GM:Studio. Each item presents a row of six boxes with geometric figures and an empty seventh box; children drag figures into the empty box. The tablet delivers "general verbal instructions", auditory feedback (a high 'pling' for correct answers), visual effects, and a four-step graduated prompts sequence from general metacognitive prompts to item-specific cognitive prompts, and automatically scores performance via log files.

Items piloted with children of the same age for suitability

title: TALKOO Arduino-based physical computing kit with multimodal learning analytics system
description: The TALKOO kit comprises pluggable hardware modules, a visual IDE and prototyping material, requiring no soldering or prior electronics knowledge; components "have the ability to talk back to the visual IDE and to a learning analytics system". Students combined the kit with craft materials to build interactive toys and motor-driven artefacts. The accompanying LAS collects ambient sensor data (colour and depth cameras with audio) and live human interaction data around an integrated screen and standing round table designed to foster collaboration.

citation: Wakefield, J., Frawley, J. K., Tyler, J., & Dyson, L. E. (2018). The impact of an iPad-supported annotation and sharing technology on university students’ learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.013
title: Affordances of tablet technology can introduce a bias towards some kinds of learning interactions over others
description: The article argues that the affordances of a technology, in the Norman (1988) sense, shape but do not dictate its educational use. The tablet's size, mobility and stylus input lend themselves to fast, structured, handwritten equation-based feedback, which "introduces a preferential bias for these types of questions over others that are less aligned". Because educators cannot fully anticipate how a tool will be appropriated in the classroom, ongoing evaluation of learning outcomes is needed rather than blanket adoption.
requirements: Deliberate, theoretically informed pedagogical design of how the technology is used in class
constraints: Neither educators nor educational technologists can know precisely how a given tool will be appropriated by instructors and students
target_learning_goals: understanding how technology affordances shape learning outcomes

citation: Quinn, D. M., Lynch, K., & Kim, J. S. (2014). Replicating the Moderating Role of Income Status on Summer School Effects across Subject Areas: A Meta-analysis. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Offer summer academic programs primarily to low-income students, who benefit more from them
description: This principle recommends directing summer math and reading programs toward low-income student populations, because recent meta-analytic evidence shows they derive larger benefit from such programs than higher-income peers. The article reports that low-income students benefit more "in both math and reading," reversing the pattern in Cooper et al.'s (2000) earlier review. It extends the authors' prior reading-only meta-analysis (Kim & Quinn, 2013) to math and supports the policy use of summer school as a compensatory lever for disadvantaged students.
requirements: Classroom- or home-based summer reading or school-based math interventions in the United States or Canada, assessed with standardized tests
Sufficient information to compute Cohen's d and a treatment/control comparison
constraints: The math evidence base is thin: "the number of studies on the effects of math summer school is low," limiting moderator analyses and statistical power
target_learners: Kindergarten to Grade 8 students in the United States and Canada
target_learning_goals: Math and reading achievement over the summer vacation months
examples: In the within-study analyses, low-income students in the same programs outperformed their higher-income peers in both math and reading; the between-study math moderator showed low-income samples at d=0.11 versus mixed-income samples at d=-0.02

article_title: Effectiveness of the flipped classroom in medical education: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Wu Yaqiu, Cheng Meixiong. (2026). Effectiveness of the flipped classroom in medical education: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09526-8
title: Tailor flipped-classroom implementation to learner stage, course objectives, and available resources rather than assuming a uniform effect
description: Because pooled benefits in medical education come with very high heterogeneity and context-dependent effect sizes, the review recommends that "implementation should be tailored to learner stage, course objectives, and available resources rather than assuming a uniform effect across settings". Residents, particularly for procedural/technical skills and satisfaction, showed the largest benefits, so stage-specific deployment is advised. The review also suggests clear course structure and learning/technical support to reduce early adaptation burden.
requirements: Clear course structure and appropriate learning and technical support to reduce transition costs and improve adherence during adoption
constraints: Effects are context dependent; key outcomes (procedural/technical skills, self-directed learning) rest on k ≤ 4 studies; residents' larger effects partly rest on single studies and are exploratory
examples: The review found larger resident effects for procedural/technical skills (between-subgroup p = 0.0131) and satisfaction (p = 0.0107), and recommends prioritizing under-studied domains in future studies

title: Tailor digital teaching methods to the specific practical skills being taught, making use of available resources
description: The review's closing design recommendation is that digital teaching methods for practical skills should not be adopted generically but matched to the concrete hands-on procedure being trained and to the resources an institution has. It states that "Digital teaching methods should be specifically tailored to the practical skills being taught, making use of available resources." This follows its finding that different interventions suit different skills, e.g. simulators for surgical procedures and video-based teaching in nursing.

target_learning_goals: patient-oriented, manual and technical practical skills

citation: Maes M, Van Gerven JD, Willaert R, Jacobs R. (2026). Augmented and virtual reality in dental and oral and maxillofacial surgery education: a systematic review with a taxonomy of training technologies. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08561-1
title: Three-category taxonomy of AR/VR training technologies: haptic simulators, head-mounted devices, and software platforms
description: The review establishes a taxonomy classifying AR/VR educational interventions into three groups. As the authors state, different AR and VR tools were "categorized into three groups: haptic simulators, head-mounted devices, and software platforms". Haptic simulators are high-fidelity VR systems providing force-feedback; head-mounted displays offer immersive 3D visual environments often without tactile feedback; software-based platforms run on standard computers, tablets, or smartphones without specialized hardware. The taxonomy was applied to the 25 included randomized controlled trials and detailed in Tables 3, 4 and 5.
requirements: Studies must involve an AR/VR/XR component and dental or OMFS learners to be classified within the taxonomy
constraints: The taxonomy was developed from 25 RCTs published between January 2015 and April 2025 in dentistry and OMFS education only
target_learners: Postgraduate residents and fellows in dentistry and OMFS
