description: The review organizes the gamified TEFL literature around a taxonomy of game elements, counting the frequency with which each appears across the 33 included studies: "Feedback	23", challenge, points, leaderboard, leveling, time, badge, progress bar, story/narration, digital badges, avatar/character, and competition. article_title: Using a Single Model Trained across Multiple Experiments to Improve the Detection of Treatment Effects
citation: Thanaporn Patikorn, Douglas Selent, Neil T. Heffernan, Joseph E. Beck, Jian Zou. (2016). Using a Single Model Trained across Multiple Experiments to Improve the Detection of Treatment Effects. Proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Educational Data Mining. https://sites.google.com/site/tamemethod/
title: TAME: detecting treatment effects by training a model across multiple experiments and testing residuals
description: TAME is a statistical method for detecting treatment effects in randomized controlled experiments run inside online tutoring systems. It borrows the idea of meta-analysis: it first models the outcome measure in the absence of condition assignment, training on all experiments in a group except the test experiment, then computes residuals (actual minus modeled outcome) for the test experiment and runs a two-tailed unpaired T-test on residuals of control versus treatment groups. The sign of the residual matters: positive residuals indicate students overperformed the model, possibly due to helpful interventions, while negative residuals indicate underperformance, possibly caused by harmful interventions.
requirements: Requires a group of similar experiments with the same dependent measures and study design format (A/B), since experiments should be combined if they have similar research questions, populations, settings, intervention components, implementation, and dependent measures
constraints: The model must be trained on data outside the experiment of interest to ensure it does not overfit to the test experiment
target_learners: middle-school students in grades 6-8 using online tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: detecting whether an instructional intervention has a statistically significant effect on student outcome measures
examples: Applied to 22 randomized controlled experiments from the ASSISTments online learning platform, using factors such as Prior Percent Correct and Guessed Gender, with log base ten of Mastery Speed as the dependent measure

citation: Steven J. Amendum, Mary Bratsch-Hines, Lynne Vernon-Feagans. (2018). Investigating the Efficacy of a Web-Based Early Reading and Professional Development Intervention for Young English Learners. Reading Research Quarterly, 53(2). https://doi.org/10.1002/rrq.188
title: Targeted Reading Intervention (TRI) framework: diagnostic, teacher-delivered one-on-one instruction with remote webcam coaching
description: The TRI is a diagnostic early reading intervention and professional development program delivered by the classroom teacher in daily 15-minute one-on-one sessions, supported by a remote literacy coach using webcam technology for real-time interaction and feedback. Grounded in an ecological systems perspective, automaticity theory, and construction–integration theory, it aims to help teachers individualize instruction for struggling readers. The article states the TRI "uses a diagnostic teaching approach to help classroom teachers improve the reading skills of students who are struggling with reading acquisition". It was designed for the general education classroom, not specifically for ELs.
requirements: Teachers work individually with one struggling reader for 15 minutes three or four times per week until the student makes rapid progress, then move to another struggling reader
A literacy coach meets weekly (later biweekly) with each teacher via webcam to observe, provide feedback, and scaffold instruction using the TRI Diagnostic Map
constraints: The TRI was designed for use in the general education classroom and was not developed specifically for English learners
target_learners: English learners in early elementary grades
target_learning_goals: word-level decoding and automatic word recognition
examples: In past randomized controlled trials the TRI produced effect sizes of .30 to .70 for struggling readers, and nonstruggling readers in TRI classrooms profited with effect sizes of .30 to .40

article_title: Skill Moderators of the Effects of a Reading Comprehension Intervention
citation: Nathan H. Clemens, Eric Oslund, Oi-man Kwok, Melissa Fogarty, Deborah Simmons, and John L. Davis. (2019). Skill Moderators of the Effects of a Reading Comprehension Intervention. Exceptional Children, 85(2), 197–211. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402918787339
title: Tailor multicomponent reading interventions so components are emphasized based on students' entry-level skill profiles
description: The article proposes that multicomponent interventions need not be delivered identically to all students: depending on the skill profiles of subgroups, certain components should be emphasized over others. It suggests that with CCT, "greater overall treatment effects may have been observed if students with stronger initial text-reading fluency skills were advanced to lessons in which text was longer and more complex". It cites Connor et al. (2011) as showing that aligning instruction to entry-level skill profiles is associated with compelling achievement effects.
requirements: Moderation analyses with measures representing the hypothesized moderating constructs to identify relevant skill profiles
constraints: The tailoring proposal is speculative; the article did not test adapted implementation, and the CCT intervention was not implemented to the extent planned
examples: The article suggests students with stronger initial text-reading fluency could skip decoding or fluency activities in favor of higher-order comprehension instruction, or that a standard intervention could be run short-term and then adapted for subgroups after a prespecified period

citation: Al Otaiba, S., Petscher, Y., Wanzek, J., Lan, P., & Rivas, B. (2018). I'm not throwing away my shot: What Alexander Hamilton can tell us about standard reading interventions. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 33(3), 156–167. https://doi.org/10.1111/ldrp.12179
title: Taxonomy of Intervention Intensity as a framework for intensifying standard reading interventions
description: The article applies Fuchs, Fuchs, & Malone's (2017) Taxonomy of Intervention Intensity as "a framework and process for teachers and schools to intensify intervention" when a standard protocol proves insufficient. Its dimensions include strength (evidence the program is validated for students with particular needs), dosage (more duration, frequency, or smaller group size), alignment (targeting appropriate skills and current performance levels), scaffolding attention to transfer, comprehensiveness (explicit, systematic instruction with modeling, immediate corrective feedback, and cumulative review), behavior supports for self-regulation and motivation, and individualization through data-based individualization with frequent progress monitoring.
requirements: Use requires monitoring student response through frequent progress monitoring and making ongoing adjustments as skill levels and demands change
constraints: The article presents the taxonomy as a framework for intensifying interventions like Passport for students with very poor comprehension skills, not as a tested manipulation in this study
target_learners: Upper elementary students with severe reading comprehension difficulties (at or below the 15th percentile)
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension, vocabulary, word reading, and reading fluency
examples: The authors suggest students may need more intervention in duration, frequency, or smaller group size, and that teachers could fine-tune alignment if groups were smaller and more homogeneous in needs

citation: Andy Bown. (2017). Elaborative Feedback to Enhance Online Second Language Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n12p164
title: Tailor elaborative feedback in online L2 reading exercises to the proficiency level of the intended readers
description: Because elaborative feedback acts as scaffolding, the article recommends that instructors and designers consider the readers' L2 reading proficiency level, the difficulty of the reading task, and models of L2 reading comprehension when writing feedback. The study showed feedback that enhanced lower-proficiency comprehension was less useful for higher-proficiency readers, so feedback should be matched to learner needs.

constraints: In heterogeneous contexts a single feedback version may not suit all learners
examples: In homogeneous classes elaborative feedback might support a large percentage of learners; in heterogeneous contexts it might be used to provide additional support to specific groups of learners.

citation: Wolf, S., Aber, J. L., Torrente, C., Rasheed, D., & McCoy, M. (2014). Cluster randomized trial of a large-scale education initiative in the Democratic Republic of Congo: Pilot year impacts on teacher development. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org

article_title: Effects of a Target-Task Problem-Solving Model on Senior Secondary School Students' Performance in Physics
citation: Olaniyan, A. O., & Omosewo, E. O. (2015). Effects of a Target-Task Problem-Solving Model on Senior Secondary School Students' Performance in Physics. Science Education International, 25(4), 522-538.
title: The Target-Task Model: a six-stage guided-discovery problem-solving model for teaching science
description: The Target-Task Model is "an adaptation of the guided discovery method for teaching science", involving presentation of a major problem whose solution requires rules and principles students may not know. It proceeds through six stages drawn from Frost (2004): Pre-task, Task, Planning, Report, Analysis and Practice. In this study it was operationalized as the Target-Task Instructional Model, with students solving mathematical and non-mathematical problems in groups of two to four while the teacher monitors, then presenting written solutions for class critique and teacher-led analysis.
requirements: The teacher presents solutions similar to the target task and guides students; the teacher introduces the topic and states objectives before the task stage
constraints: The model was studied only in senior secondary physics, on current electricity concepts, over four teaching weeks
examples: In the study, the experimental teacher used a step-by-step instructional package covering Pre-task, Task, Planning and Presentation, Report, Analysis and Practice stages for current electricity

citation: Berat Ahi. (2017). The Effect of Talking Drawings on Five-Year-Old Turkish Children’s Mental Models of the Water Cycle. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 12(3), 349-367.
title: The talking drawings technique proceeds through six stages combining individual drawing, peer discussion, source reading and re-drawing
description: The talking drawings technique, developed by McConnel (1993), elicits the pictures in children's minds related to a phenomenon and then develops these pictures through drawing and dialogue. The article presents it as a six-stage sequence: "The children create their drawings related to the topic", discuss them in pairs, hear selected source books with visuals, revisit and re-draw, then compare first and second drawings in child-centered discussion. In the study it was completed over three sessions in a seven-hour period.
requirements: Requires drawing and speaking skills, which the article says makes it quite suitable for use with young children

constraints: In the study it was applied to the water cycle with five-year-olds in a Turkish preschool; the author notes a need for research at different levels of schooling
examples: In the study, session one held a large group discussion and initial drawings, session two used book reading and visuals, and session three had children re-draw, compare drawings and explain differences to the whole class

citation: Avci Akbel, B. (2018). A review on effectiveness of cello etudes created for longas and syrtos. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 75, 1-18. https://www.ejer.com.tr
title: Etude-writing model adapted from the Taba-Tyler model with four programming steps
description: The article adapts the Taba-Tyler curriculum model into a procedure for designing piece-specific instrumental etudes. It states that "the following basic steps of programming must be followed when designing an etude": identifying requirements, identifying the distant goal and objectives, selecting and arranging content, and selecting and arranging learning experiences. In this study the steps were instantiated from expert interviews, researcher observation, and analysis of the target pieces, producing etudes that followed the 'known to unknown' and 'simple to complex' principles with written explanations under each exercise.
requirements: Expert input to identify the technical challenges the etudes must address
Analysis of the target musical pieces, transposed into bass clef and a cello-suitable key
Written explanations under each exercise describing the behaviors to be improved
constraints: Developed and evaluated for cello performance of Longa and Syrto forms in Turkish Music with eight conservatory students
target_learners: senior undergraduate and graduate cello students at Turkish music conservatories
target_learning_goals: overcoming technical and musical performance difficulties in Turkish Music pieces, including coordination between the right hand and the bow, détaché bow technique, and transitions between strings
examples: Preparatory exercises were created based on expert-identified challenges in détaché bow technique, bow-string coordination, and string transitions, then tested against control-group practice of the pieces

article_title: The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students' Performance in Fractions
citation: Charalambos Lemonidis & Ioanna Kaiafa. (2019). The Effect of Using Storytelling Strategy on Students’ Performance in Fractions. Journal of Education and Learning, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v8n2p165
title: Target-focused picture stories for teaching fractions (unit-fraction protagonist narrative in seven episodes)
description: The intervention material for the experimental group was a set of target-focused picture stories written in accordance with the curriculum objectives for rational numbers. Each story is "a narrative unit that includes seven episodes", whose protagonist is "a unit fraction that wants to raise his value in order to be accepted by his parents and teachers", helped by two whole numbers, 3 and 5. Students watch the characters' adventures while learning fractions and their properties, and the stories open discussion of friendship, companionship and diversity.
requirements: Stories must be target-focused, i.e. in accordance with the curriculum objectives for rational number teaching
examples: The teacher read the story to students while pictures accompanying the text were displayed, followed by a brief discussion and story-related math activities

article_title: Assessment of Conventional Teaching Procedures: Implications for Gifted Learners
citation: Mogbel Aid K Alenizi. (2016). Assessment of Conventional Teaching Procedures: Implications for Gifted Learners. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 4(3), 8-17. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.4n.3p.8
title: Task analysis as a teaching method: breaking skills into teachable subskills
description: The article defines the task analysis method as dividing skills into units or secondary skills that can be taught, so students first master simple components and then combine them into a clear, fluent, sequential whole skill. It is presented as a useful solution that lets the student succeed on parts of a concept skill and helps identify the area the student failed in and the parts of the task where the student faces difficulty in mastering, so those parts can be practised specially. In this study it was consolidated with process training in the experimental programme.
requirements: The teacher must identify the area that the student failed in and the parts of the task where the student faces difficulty in mastering
constraints: The article states the strategy requires the presence of a weakness or developmental disability whose problem includes limited education and experience in the task itself
target_learners: students with maths learning disorders at foundation/elementary level
target_learning_goals: numerical skills including counting, number concepts, symbols and calculating processes
examples: The researcher broke down the skills that the child failed at in order to identify a series of behavioural and knowledge skills required to conduct those skills

article_title: Pragmatic Comprehension Development through Telecollaboration
citation: Vahid Rafieyan, Maryam Sharafi-Nejad, Zahra Khavari, Lin Siew Eng & Abdul Rashid Mohamed. (2014). Pragmatic Comprehension Development through Telecollaboration. English Language Teaching, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n2p11
title: 30-item multiple choice pragmatic listening comprehension test (Taguchi 2007, 2008)
description: The outcome measure: a 30-item multiple choice pragmatic listening comprehension test developed by Taguchi (2007, 2008), containing 24 experimental items testing comprehension of implied opinions and 6 literal items used as distractors. Each item presents a conversation between a female and a male native English speaker with four choices. Validity was judged by two pragmatics experts; split-half reliability was 0.80 in a pilot with 20 non-participant undergraduates.
requirements: Expert content validation of items
Pilot administration to establish split-half reliability
constraints: The 6 literal distractor items were excluded from analysis, so scores ranged 0 to 24
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of pragmatically implied opinions in listening
examples: Each correct answer on the 24 experimental items was assigned 1 mark; the 6 literal items were excluded as distractors.

article_title: Improvement of the Robotics Cross-Cutting Course for Training of Specialists in Professions of the Future
citation: Elena V. Soboleva, Nikita L. Karavaev, Nadezhda V. Shalaginova, Marina S. Perevozchikova. (2018). Improvement of the Robotics Cross-Cutting Course for Training of Specialists in Professions of the Future. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(4). https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.4.845
title: A cross-cutting robotics course designed around a core system of specially selected tasks spanning preschool, school and university levels
description: The article's redesigned methodology places a system of tasks at the core of the robotics course, with new knowledge acquired through solving problems rather than through fixed content sequences. As the authors state, "The main point of the task approach is that the acquisition of new knowledge occurs through the process of cognitive activity in solving the problem, which is set by a system of specially selected tasks." Tasks are organised in tables by competence (systems thinking, programming/artificial intelligence, project management, cross-industry communication) and by educational level, using medical-robotics problem situations. The set is explicitly not universal; it demonstrates the possibility of composing such a system.
requirements: Learning objectives are replaced by cross-professional competences, and the place-in-course and tools components are qualified by students themselves
constraints: The presented set of tasks does not pretend to be universal and ultimate; it demonstrates didactic potential for improving the existing robotics training path
examples: Table 1 sets systems-thinking tasks from describing inputs and outputs of a thermometer in preschool to building an expert system diagnosing a respiratory disease at university level; Table 4 sets cross-industry tasks in biology, ecology and physics such as an automated fire safety system

citation: Milosevic, D. (2017). Using video materials in English for technical sciences: a case study. In C. Sarré & S. Whyte (Eds), New developments in ESP teaching and learning research (pp. 15-30). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2017.cssw2017.743
title: Tarnopolsky's constructivist blended learning approach to ESP
description: Tarnopolsky's constructivist blended learning approach combines traditional methods with modern web-based technologies, stressing the importance of practical experience in e-learning. As a supporter of the input-output theory, the author proposes an entire set of ESP activities (role-plays, case studies, simulations, etc.) with recommendations for integration of the four skills. The approach states that "successful knowledge and skills constructing is achieved owing to students' regular Internet research on professional sites in English".
requirements: Students must engage in regular Internet research on professional sites in English
examples: The small-scale study relied on this approach by implementing internet resources as instructional materials and employing post-viewing activities.

title: Tailor consultation intensity to teachers' baseline knowledge, skills, and beliefs rather than providing the same support to all
description: The article recommends matching consultative resources to teacher profiles: teachers with no barriers benefited equally from best-practice consultation, while teachers with knowledge, belief, and skill barriers benefited most from the multi-component package. The authors state that "identifying those teachers who are most in need of comprehensive consultation could make the use of consultants more efficient." This principle operationalizes the theory of change by assessing baseline knowledge, skills, and beliefs and allocating intensive multi-component support only where barriers are present.
requirements: Reliable and valid tools for measuring teacher knowledge, skills, and beliefs, which the authors say require additional research
constraints: The authors note support for the theory of change relies on interpretation of trends rather than statistical significance pending a large clinical trial

target_learning_goals: improved implementation integrity of classroom interventions
examples: The study block-randomized teachers within schools on baseline competence and used latent class analysis plus median splits on baseline skills to identify which teacher profiles benefited from the multi-component condition

article_title: The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives
citation: Shadi Rastegaran. (2016). The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(2), 18-24. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.18
title: Task-based language teaching: tasks as the core unit of planning with learner-centred, meaning-focused characteristics
description: The article presents task-based language teaching (TBLT) as "an approach based on the use of tasks as the core unit of planning and instruction in language teaching". Tasks are activities requiring comprehending, producing, manipulating or interacting in authentic language with attention primarily on meaning, and a task "has a nonlinguistic outcome while an exercise has a linguistic outcome". The article lists TBLT characteristics including emphasis on target-language interaction, authentic texts, focus on the learning process itself, enhancing learners' own personal experiences, and linking classroom language with language outside the classroom.
requirements: A skillful and responsive teacher able to cope with groups of learners
Teacher selects, adapts, or creates tasks based on learners' needs, interests, and language skill level
constraints: As described in the article, applied to second-language vocabulary instruction
target_learning_goals: Communicative language use and vocabulary learning
examples: The study operationalised an authentic task as reading zodiac-sign texts and writing personal descriptions, against a traditional dictionary-extract control condition

citation: Michael L. Pate, Greg Miller. (2011). Effects of Think–Aloud Pair Problem Solving on Secondary–Level Students’ Performance in Career and Technical Education Courses. Journal of Agricultural Education. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2011.01120
title: Adopt TAPPS at the secondary level for purposes other than raising success rate or reducing completion time
description: The authors tentatively conclude that TAPPS "may not be an appropriate strategy at the secondary level if the agricultural instructors’ focus is a higher success rate and a reduction in the time to complete the task." However, they state instructors may have other legitimate reasons for using it, such as facilitating collaborative learning or identifying student misunderstandings to inform individualized or group instructional interventions.
requirements: Instructors should have goals beyond success rate and completion time, such as diagnosis of student misunderstandings
constraints: Not supported as a means of raising troubleshooting success rates or reducing completion time at the secondary level based on this exploratory study
target_learners: secondary-level agricultural education and CTE students
examples: The study used TAPPS with randomly assigned listening partners and audio recording to verify treatment fidelity across five Iowa secondary schools.

article_title: A Feasibility Study of Task-Based Teaching of College English Writing in Chinese EFL Context
citation: Linying Cao. (2012). A Feasibility Study of Task-based Teaching of College English Writing in Chinese EFL Context. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p80
title: Task-based EFL writing lesson pattern: pre-task preparation, task-planning-report cycle, and language focus
description: The article operationalizes Willis' framework for writing classrooms as a reusable lesson pattern. Preparatory activities precede a specific writing task; students then discuss the task orally in pairs or groups, plan outlines and notes, draft collaboratively, exchange drafts with another pair or group for improvement suggestions, redraft into final versions, and present reports to the class, with the teacher summing up noteworthy points. The core is the task cycle, where fluency dominates the task and planning stages while the report demands accurate grammatical forms.
requirements: Pairs or groups for oral discussion and collaborative drafting
Time limits for first drafts
An audience (the rest of the class) for final drafts and reports
constraints: The article does not address task complexity, task difficulty or task production in its task design
examples: Drafts were exchanged with another pair or group asking for suggestions for improvements before final drafts were made ready for audience

article_title: Effects of Character Education on the Self-Esteem of Intellectually Able and Less Able Elementary Students in Kuwait
citation: Tannir, A., & Al-Hroub, A. (2013). Effects of character education on the self-esteem of intellectually able and less able elementary students in Kuwait. International Journal of Special Education, 28(1), 47-59.
title: Character education programs should be tailored to different ability levels rather than delivered uniformly
description: The study found that a uniform character education program produced divergent effects by ability group: it benefited intellectually less able students while slightly reducing self-esteem among intellectually able students. The article argues that "character education, when taught, is delivered using the same approach for all students. It does not take into account different ability levels and how to address their needs." Differentiated implementation is needed so that programs serve both groups effectively.
requirements: Programs must assess students' intellectual ability levels before implementation to anticipate differential effects.
constraints: Findings come from one bilingual school with a small sample (N=39) and a five-week intervention, limiting generalizability.
target_learners: Intellectually able and less able students
examples: The study delivered the same character education activities to both ability subgroups and found opposite self-esteem outcomes for each.

description: The article uses nine tales of virtue, fictional stories based on King Bhumibol Adulyadej's teachings, as reading material alongside DR-TA. article_title: Talk for Writing: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Julie Dockrell, Chloë Marshall and Dominic Wyse. (2015). Talk for Writing: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: The 3Is framework: imitation, innovation and invention as a developmental scaffold for writing
description: The 3Is framework is the distinctive pedagogical structure of Talk for Writing, in which pupils move from learning texts by heart (imitation), to adapting known stories to create their own versions (innovation), to composing original writing (invention). The article states that "The 3Is framework entails working from (1) Imitation, to (2) Innovation, and finally to (3) Invention in children’s writing" and regards it as a way of scaffolding the writing process, with responsibility shifting from teacher to pupil. The evaluators note the first two phases are unique to the approach, while invention is common later primary practice, and question whether the framework matches the original scaffolding concept's timescales.
requirements: Whole-school adoption of the framework, with teachers trained through the Primary Writing Project and a literacy lead responsible for implementation
constraints: The evaluators note the framework's phases are conceived over much longer timescales than the original scaffolding concept envisaged, and the literature review found no evidence that daily repetition of texts supports writing skills
target_learners: Primary school pupils from nursery to Year 6
target_learning_goals: Understanding the structure and elements of written language

article_title: Talk for Writing: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Julie Dockrell, Chloë Marshall and Dominic Wyse. (2015). Talk for Writing: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Talk for Writing whole-school programme and its Primary Writing Project non-negotiables
description: Talk for Writing is a universal, whole-school approach to teaching primary writing, delivered within the Primary Writing Project professional development package. Schools commit to non-negotiable components; the article states "The main non- negotiables contained seven elements related to written text production", including adoption of the 3Is, daily shared writing, visible common practice such as story maps and boxing up, systematic word and sentence level teaching, a school-wide text framework, writing for audiences and purposes, and regular formative assessment. Each school appointed a literacy lead responsible for implementation, supported by leadership training days and whole-school conferences.
requirements: Head teachers, all teachers and teaching assistants commit to attending training days and using Talk for Writing; each school identifies a literacy lead
constraints: The programme was still in development during the evaluation, and the review found no objective marking frame provided for assessing writing progress
target_learners: Primary school pupils from nursery to Year 6 in disadvantaged areas
target_learning_goals: Writing attainment at word, sentence and text level
examples: The pilot ran for 18 months from January 2013 to July 2014 in ten Portsmouth schools, with six full days for leadership teams plus three whole-school Big Days

article_title: Animation Based Learning of Electronic Devices
citation: Gero, A., Zoabi, W., & Sabag, N. (2014). Animation Based Learning of Electronic Devices. Advances in Engineering Education, 4(1), Winter 2014. https://journals.gmu.edu/aaa/issue/winter-2014
title: Include teacher-presented computer animations tailored to students' background when teaching the operation principles of electronic devices.
description: The article recommends that "we recommend that our colleagues include animations, developed with an eye toward the students' background, when teaching the operation principles of electronic devices such as the bipolar junction transistor". The animation should refrain from advanced terms, rely on qualitative analysis, and be designed in light of Mayer and Moreno's principles.
requirements: The animation must be tailored to the students' background and qualitatively describe the processes occurring in the device.
The teacher should accompany the animation with verbal explanations to clarify its limitations and call attention to key details.
constraints: Existing animations may be too simplistic or at a university level requiring advanced mathematical and physical knowledge.
target_learning_goals: understanding the principle of operation of the bipolar junction transistor
examples: The researchers developed a new learning unit based on Microsoft PowerPoint that took 100 hours, based on the Sedra and Smith textbook and designed in light of the principles of Mayer and Moreno and Kali and Linn.

constraints: Findings are based on within-treatment group analyses of a quasi-experimental design

examples: The 4Rs+MTP program combines a literacy-based SEL curriculum with video-based coaching to improve teacher-student interactions

nurses, midwives, clinical officers, and pediatric health professionals

citation: Mohar Sebastian, Crawford Ana María, Vásquez Ulises Sánchez, Serna-Muñoz Ricardo, Martínez Rodrigo Rubio. (2026). The educational impact of a serious game for airway management skills of medical trainees. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09552-6

description: The article supports tabletop serious games as practical, low-cost complements to conventional airway training. title: Targeted Double Scoring (TDS): a decision-theoretic methodology that restricts double scoring to Critical Score Ranges near the pass/fail cutoff
description: TDS is a scoring-assignment methodology in which a first rater scores every performance, and only examinees whose Rater 1 score falls within a Critical Score Range (CSR) near the pass/fail cutoff receive a second rating. The article defines the CSR as "a specific range of scores where the risk of incorrect pass/fail decisions is highest" and selects the optimal CSR by minimizing a statistical-decision-theory loss function combining the probability of a score falling in the CSR with configured costs of false passes (LP), false fails (LF), and extra rating (c). The article positions TDS as a generalizable framework adaptable to different OSCE designs and rubrics rather than as a finding tied to its own dataset.
requirements: The article states "The foundational requirement for TDS implementation is the existing use of traditional DS within the OSCE framework."
Researcher-supplied loss constants LP, LF, and c must be set; the article used c = 40 and five conventional {LP,LF} combinations.
constraints: "While TDS offers significant cost savings, its effectiveness may vary depending on the specific context of the OSCE."
"Deciding LP and LF may be the first difficulty that researchers face when modeling the data."
CSR interval splitting poses a trade-off: intervals as fine as one point make CSRs meaningless, while wider intervals yield less rater-labor savings.
In this study's FS station, no {LP,LF} combination favored TDS over the baseline.

target_learning_goals: reliable and fair pass/fail decisions on clinical skills performance assessment at controlled cost
examples: Applied to a pilot remote OSCE of 550 Chinese clinical medicine undergraduates with three stations (CR, PE, FS), a cut-off of 60 out of 100, and two remote raters per performance.

description: TAME-ChatGPT is a validated survey instrument based on the technology acceptance model designed to assess university students' attitudes towards and adoption of ChatGPT. article_title: Health literacy competency requirements for health professionals: a Delphi consensus study in Taiwan.
citation: Tsai Han-Yi, Lee Shoou-Yih D., Coleman Cliff, Sørensen Kristine, Tsai Tzu-I. (2024). Health literacy competency requirements for health professionals: a Delphi consensus study in Taiwan. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05198-4
title: Validated set of 42 health literacy competencies (knowledge, attitudes, skills) plus 32 ranked practices for health professionals
description: This study delivers a cross-culturally translated, Delphi-validated set of health literacy competencies for health professionals, organized as knowledge items (e.g., K2 "knows which kinds of words, phrases, or concepts may be jargon to patients"), attitude items (e.g., non-judgmental, empathic attitudes), and skill items (e.g., S13 teach-back, S21 analogies). target_learning_goals: Health literacy knowledge, attitudes, and communication skills for clinical encounters with patients with limited health literacy
examples: Round 3 merged three similar skill items into one; final set includes 12 knowledge, 9 attitude, and 21 skill items, with Table 5 printing original and Traditional Chinese versions of the 32 ranked practices.

citation: Thielmann Anika, Schmitz Marie-Therese, Welchowski Thomas, Weltermann Birgitta. (2024). Effectiveness of the online-eLearning program KeepCoool at improving the vaccine cold chain in general practices. PLoS ONE 19(4): e0301847. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0301847
title: Tailored learning: individualizing information to improve behavior change in eLearning
description: The article frames KeepCoool within the didactic shift away from one-size-fits-all approaches toward learner-adaptive approaches. "Tailored learning involves the individualization of information for each participant to reach better results regarding the desired behavior change"; it is discussed that individualization increases acceptability of information so that it is more frequently remembered and discussed. KeepCoool applied this via professional-group targeting, feedback tailored to baseline knowledge, and personal address.
requirements: Tailoring requires knowledge of each participant's baseline knowledge and professional group, obtained here through the 11-item pre-test.
constraints: The article does not test tailoring as a separate factor; it is an authors' design rationale attributed to the literature, not a measured component in this study.
target_learners: trainees differing in knowledge and experience
examples: KeepCoool used personal address, profession-specific targeting, and individualized feedback as its three didactic elements.

title: Design teaching strategies tailored to students' own e-learning strategies to promote learning and academic achievement
description: The article recommends that educators and policy makers use knowledge of the strategies students actually adopt in e-learning to shape instruction. This includes supporting students who lack self-regulation skills and remain passive, and embedding peer learning more explicitly into courses.

article_title: E-learning intention of students with anxiety: Evidence from the first wave of COVID-19 pandemic in China.
citation: Hu Xuan, Zhang Jiaqi, He Shuang, Zhu Ruilin, Shen Shan, Liu Bingsheng. (2022). E-learning intention of students with anxiety: Evidence from the first wave of COVID-19 pandemic in China. Journal of Affective Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jad.2022.04.121
title: Technology Acceptance Model extended with a synthesized view of general anxiety for e-learning intention
description: The article applies the Technology Acceptance Model, in which e-learning acceptance is determined by behavioral intention explained by perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, where PU refers to "a user believes in the existence of a positive use-performance" and PEOU to the effortlessness of use. Its contribution is classifying students by the GAD-2 scale and comparing TAM paths between anxiety and non-anxiety groups, showing the model holds for anxious students while PU effects strengthen and PEOU effects weaken. The authors argue this synthesized (non-computer-specific) anxiety view enhances TAM's explanatory scope.
requirements: Measurement of anxiety via a validated screening instrument (the article used GAD-2 with cut-off 3) and TAM construct measures adapted to the e-learning context
constraints: The study does not model anxiety as an external variable in the TAM, and the different anxiety sources are synthesized rather than separated
target_learning_goals: e-learning continuance intention and technology acceptance
examples: SEM analysis of 512 survey responses with GAD-2 classification into anxiety (N = 368) and non-anxiety (N = 144) groups

article_title: Learning clinical skills: an ecological perspective.
citation: Brymer, E., & Schweitzer, R. D. (2022). Learning clinical skills: an ecological perspective. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 27(3), 691-707. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-022-10115-9
title: Design clinical learning around manipulating task constraints while preserving task representativeness
description: The article recommends that clinical educators deliberately manipulate task constraints — goals, boundaries, scenario restrictions, equipment — as the primary lever for shaping learning, since "Manipulating task constraints is the simplest way to change learners' behaviours from this theoretical viewpoint". Constraint manipulation must rest on task representativeness so learners attune to key affordances for real-world behaviour. It is the practical core of the ecological framework the paper advances for clinical education.
requirements: Educators need knowledge of the real-world performance constraints in the clinical context before designing tasks, and must identify which information sources are vital for each learner
constraints: The article warns that ineffective tweaks by inexperienced educators can inadvertently represent ineffective behaviours such as rigidity, and that constraints are dynamic, emerging and decaying over time, so confirmation needs to be ongoing
target_learning_goals: clinical skills including alliance-building, assessment and reflexive practice
examples: The article describes adjusting scenarios or restrictions mid-activity, manipulating boundaries in group learning, and intervening when a diagnostic-instrument task overshadowed critical thinking about diagnosis

article_title: ADHD and Academic Success in University Students: The Important Role of Impaired Attention.
citation: Henning Colin, Summerfeldt Laura J., Parker James D. A. (2021). ADHD and Academic Success in University Students: The Important Role of Impaired Attention. Journal of Attention Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547211036758
title: Post-secondary institutions should target and prioritize educational programming for inattention symptoms in at-risk students
description: The article recommends that psychoeducational programming in higher education focus specifically on inattention symptoms of ADHD rather than overall symptomatology, because inattention was the only dimension linked to both GPA and degree completion. It suggests "test and assignments accommodations and coaching" and early intervention such as "coaching and/or academic skills training" for at-risk students, regardless of prior ADHD diagnosis. The recommendation rests on the study's finding that inattention, not hyperactivity or impulsivity, drove academic underachievement.
requirements: Assessment of inattention problems among students at the start of their post-secondary programs to identify at-risk students
constraints: The article notes more research is needed to determine whether reductions in inattention symptoms following educational programs ultimately lead to greater academic success
target_learners: first-year post-secondary undergraduate students at risk of academic underachievement
students with ADHD, particularly predominantly inattentive presentation or individual education plans
examples: The article cites evaluations of organizational skills training and executive function training interventions, and peer mentoring, as programs shown to reduce ADHD symptoms and inattention-related problems among college students.
